title: Group Theory in Quantum Mechanics
text:
The connection between symmetry and quantum mechanics is one of the deepest ideas in physics. When a system possesses a symmetry — rotational, translational, or something more exotic — the consequences are immediate and powerful: conserved quantities, selection rules, and (most strikingly) exact degeneracies in the energy spectrum that persist even when we cannot solve the Schrodinger equation analytically.
The mathematical language for symmetry is group theory, and the specific tool we need is representation theory: the study of how abstract groups act on vector spaces. These notes develop the key ideas from the ground up, with an emphasis on physical applications. We assume familiarity with linear algebra and basic quantum mechanics, but not with abstract algebra.

title: Group Theory in Quantum Mechanics
text:
The connection between symmetry and quantum mechanics is one of the deepest ideas in physics. When a system possesses a symmetry — rotational, translational, or something more exotic — the consequences are immediate and powerful: conserved quantities, selection rules, and (most strikingly) exact degeneracies in the energy spectrum that persist even when we cannot solve the Schrodinger equation analytically.
The mathematical language for symmetry is group theory, and the specific tool we need is representation theory: the study of how abstract groups act on vector spaces. These notes develop the key ideas from the ground up, with an emphasis on physical applications. We assume familiarity with linear algebra and basic quantum mechanics, but not with abstract algebra.

title: Group Theory in Quantum Mechanics
text:
Groups: Definitions and Examples
A group \(G\) is a set equipped with a binary operation \(\cdot : G \times G \to G\) satisfying:

Associativity: \((g_1 \cdot g_2) \cdot g_3 = g_1 \cdot (g_2 \cdot g_3)\) for all \(g_1, g_2, g_3 \in G\).
Identity: There exists \(e \in G\) such that \(e \cdot g = g \cdot e = g\) for all \(g\).
Inverses: For every \(g \in G\), there exists \(g^{-1} \in G\) with \(g \cdot g^{-1} = g^{-1} \cdot g = e\).

If additionally \(g_1 \cdot g_2 = g_2 \cdot g_1\) for all elements, the group is abelian.
Examples in physics:

\(\mathbb{Z}_n\): cyclic group of order \(n\); discrete rotational symmetry of a regular polygon.
\(S_n\): the symmetric group on \(n\) objects; permutation symmetry of identical particles.
\(SO(3)\): the rotation group in three dimensions; symmetry of rotationally invariant Hamiltonians.
\(SU(2)\): the double cover of \(SO(3)\); the natural symmetry group for spin.
\(SU(3)\): the gauge group of QCD; its representation theory organizes the hadron spectrum.


Homomorphisms
A group homomorphism \(\phi: G \to H\) is a map respecting the group structure: \(\phi(g_1 \cdot g_2) = \phi(g_1) \cdot \phi(g_2)\). An isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism. The kernel \(\ker(\phi) = \{g \in G : \phi(g) = e_H\}\) is always a normal subgroup of \(G\).

title: Group Theory in Quantum Mechanics
text:
Representations

Definition
A representation of a group \(G\) on a vector space \(V\) is a homomorphism \[
D: G \to GL(V),
\] where \(GL(V)\) is the group of invertible linear maps on \(V\). That is, to each group element \(g\) we assign an invertible matrix \(D(g)\) such that \[
D(g_1) D(g_2) = D(g_1 g_2), \qquad D(e) = \mathbb{I}.
\]
The dimension of the representation is \(\dim V\).
Unitary representations. In quantum mechanics, we want the symmetry transformations to preserve inner products, so we require \(D(g)\) to be unitary: \(D(g)^\dagger D(g) = \mathbb{I}\). For compact groups and finite groups, every representation is equivalent to a unitary one (by averaging over the group).


Reducible and irreducible representations
A representation \(D\) on \(V\) is reducible if there exists a proper subspace \(W \subset V\) that is invariant under all \(D(g)\): \(D(g)W \subseteq W\) for all \(g \in G\). If no such subspace exists, the representation is irreducible (an irrep).
For unitary representations, reducibility implies complete reducibility: if \(W\) is invariant, then so is \(W^\perp\), and the representation decomposes as \(V = W \oplus W^\perp\). Iterating, any unitary representation of a finite or compact group decomposes into a direct sum of irreps: \[
V = \bigoplus_{\alpha} n_\alpha \, V_\alpha,
\] where \(V_\alpha\) ranges over the distinct irreps and \(n_\alpha\) is the multiplicity of \(V_\alpha\).

title: Group Theory in Quantum Mechanics
text:
Schur’s Lemma
Schur’s lemma is the single most important result in representation theory. It comes in two parts.

Statement
Part 1. Let \(D_1: G \to GL(V_1)\) and \(D_2: G \to GL(V_2)\) be irreducible representations, and let \(A: V_1 \to V_2\) be a linear map satisfying \[
A \, D_1(g) = D_2(g) \, A \qquad \text{for all } g \in G.
\] Then either \(A = 0\) or \(A\) is an isomorphism (and in particular \(\dim V_1 = \dim V_2\)).
Part 2. If \(D: G \to GL(V)\) is an irreducible representation over \(\mathbb{C}\), and \(A: V \to V\) satisfies \(A \, D(g) = D(g) \, A\) for all \(g\), then \(A = \lambda \mathbb{I}\) for some \(\lambda \in \mathbb{C}\).


Proof sketch
Part 1. Consider \(\ker(A) \subseteq V_1\). For any \(v \in \ker(A)\) and any \(g \in G\): \[
A(D_1(g)v) = D_2(g)(Av) = D_2(g) \cdot 0 = 0,
\] so \(D_1(g)v \in \ker(A)\). Thus \(\ker(A)\) is a \(G\)-invariant subspace of \(V_1\). Since \(V_1\) is irreducible, either \(\ker(A) = V_1\) (so \(A = 0\)) or \(\ker(A) = \{0\}\) (so \(A\) is injective).
Similarly, \(\mathrm{im}(A) \subseteq V_2\) is \(G\)-invariant. Since \(V_2\) is irreducible, either \(\mathrm{im}(A) = \{0\}\) (so \(A = 0\)) or \(\mathrm{im}(A) = V_2\) (so \(A\) is surjective).
Combining: \(A\) is either zero or an isomorphism. \(\blacksquare\)
Part 2. Since we are over \(\mathbb{C}\), \(A\) has at least one eigenvalue \(\lambda\). The operator \(A - \lambda\mathbb{I}\) commutes with all \(D(g)\) (since \(A\) and \(\mathbb{I}\) both do) and has a non-trivial kernel (the \(\lambda\)-eigenspace). By Part 1, \(A - \lambda\mathbb{I}\) must be zero. Hence \(A = \lambda\mathbb{I}\). \(\blacksquare\)


Physical consequence: why symmetry implies degeneracy
Part 2 of Schur’s lemma has an immediate and profound physical consequence. Suppose the Hamiltonian \(H\) commutes with all elements of a symmetry group \(G\): \[
[H, D(g)] = 0 \qquad \text{for all } g \in G.
\]
Consider an energy eigenspace \(V_E = \{|\psi\rangle : H|\psi\rangle = E|\psi\rangle\}\). Since \([H, D(g)] = 0\), the eigenspace \(V_E\) is \(G\)-invariant and carries a representation of \(G\). If this representation is irreducible with dimension \(d\), then Schur’s lemma tells us:

Any operator commuting with all \(D(g)\) acts as a scalar on \(V_E\).

In particular, \(H\) acts as the scalar \(E\) on the entire \(d\)-dimensional space. The degeneracy of the energy level \(E\) is at least the dimension of the irreducible representation. This degeneracy is exact and does not require any perturbative or approximate reasoning — it follows purely from the symmetry.
Conversely, if we observe a \(d\)-fold degeneracy in a system with symmetry group \(G\), we know the degenerate states must transform as an irrep of \(G\) with dimension \(d\). This is why representation theory is the natural language for organizing quantum mechanical spectra.

title: Group Theory in Quantum Mechanics
text:
SU(2) and Angular Momentum

The algebra
The group \(SU(2)\) is the most important symmetry group in quantum mechanics. Its Lie algebra \(\mathfrak{su}(2)\) is spanned by the angular momentum operators \(J_x, J_y, J_z\) satisfying \[
[J_i, J_j] = i \epsilon_{ijk} J_k.
\]
The Casimir operator \(\mathbf{J}^2 = J_x^2 + J_y^2 + J_z^2\) commutes with all \(J_i\) and therefore, by Schur’s lemma, acts as a scalar on each irrep.


Irreducible representations
The irreps of \(SU(2)\) are labeled by \(j = 0, \frac{1}{2}, 1, \frac{3}{2}, 2, \ldots\) and have dimension \(2j+1\). Within the irrep labeled by \(j\), the states are \(|j, m\rangle\) with \(m = -j, -j+1, \ldots, j-1, j\), and the operators act as: \[
\mathbf{J}^2 |j,m\rangle = j(j+1)|j,m\rangle, \qquad J_z |j,m\rangle = m|j,m\rangle,
\] \[
J_\pm |j,m\rangle = \sqrt{j(j+1) - m(m \pm 1)} \, |j, m \pm 1\rangle,
\] where \(J_\pm = J_x \pm iJ_y\) are the raising and lowering operators.
Integer \(j\): These correspond to genuine representations of \(SO(3)\) (the rotation group). They describe orbital angular momentum.
Half-integer \(j\): These are projective representations of \(SO(3)\) (or equivalently, genuine representations of \(SU(2)\), the double cover). They describe spin. Under a \(2\pi\) rotation, a state with half-integer \(j\) picks up a factor of \((-1)\), which is invisible in expectation values but detectable in interference experiments.


Angular momentum addition
The problem of adding angular momenta — combining two systems with spins \(j_1\) and \(j_2\) — is the problem of decomposing the tensor product \(j_1 \otimes j_2\) into irreps.
Clebsch–Gordan decomposition: \[
j_1 \otimes j_2 = |j_1 - j_2| \;\oplus\; (|j_1 - j_2| + 1) \;\oplus\; \cdots \;\oplus\; (j_1 + j_2).
\]
The total angular momentum \(J\) ranges from \(|j_1 - j_2|\) to \(j_1 + j_2\) in integer steps, and each value appears exactly once. The change-of-basis coefficients are the Clebsch–Gordan coefficients: \[
|J, M\rangle = \sum_{m_1 + m_2 = M} \langle j_1, m_1; j_2, m_2 | J, M\rangle \, |j_1, m_1\rangle \otimes |j_2, m_2\rangle.
\]
Dimension check: \(\sum_{J=|j_1-j_2|}^{j_1+j_2}(2J+1) = (2j_1+1)(2j_2+1)\), confirming the decomposition accounts for all states.
Example: Two spin-\(1/2\) particles. \(\frac{1}{2} \otimes \frac{1}{2} = 0 \oplus 1\). The triplet (\(J=1\), three states: \(|1,1\rangle, |1,0\rangle, |1,-1\rangle\)) and the singlet (\(J=0\), one state: \(|0,0\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|\!\uparrow\downarrow\rangle - |\!\downarrow\uparrow\rangle)\)). The \(4 = 3 + 1\) decomposition is the starting point for understanding the helium atom, the deuteron, and countless other two-particle systems.

title: Group Theory in Quantum Mechanics
text:
The Wigner-Eckart Theorem
The Wigner-Eckart theorem is one of the most powerful consequences of rotational symmetry in quantum mechanics. It factorizes the matrix elements of any operator that transforms in a definite way under rotations into a geometric part (a Clebsch-Gordan coefficient that encodes the angular momentum coupling) and a dynamical part (a reduced matrix element that encodes the physics specific to the system).

Spherical tensor operators
An operator \(T^{(k)}_q\) (with \(q = -k, -k+1, \ldots, k\)) is called a spherical tensor operator of rank \(k\) if it transforms under rotations in the same way as the angular momentum eigenstates \(|k, q\rangle\). Precisely, this means it satisfies the commutation relations \[
[J_z, T^{(k)}_q] = q \, T^{(k)}_q, \qquad [J_\pm, T^{(k)}_q] = \sqrt{k(k+1) - q(q \pm 1)} \; T^{(k)}_{q \pm 1}.
\]
These relations say that the \((2k+1)\) components \(\{T^{(k)}_q\}\) transform among themselves under rotations exactly as an irrep of spin \(k\). Equivalently, under a finite rotation \(R\) implemented by the unitary operator \(\mathcal{D}(R)\), \[
\mathcal{D}(R) \, T^{(k)}_q \, \mathcal{D}(R)^\dagger = \sum_{q'} D^{(k)}_{q'q}(R) \; T^{(k)}_{q'},
\] where \(D^{(k)}_{q'q}(R)\) are the Wigner \(D\)-matrix elements.
Examples of spherical tensor operators:

Rank 0 (\(k=0\)): A scalar operator, e.g., \(\mathbf{J}^2\) or the Hamiltonian of a rotationally invariant system. It has a single component \(T^{(0)}_0\) that commutes with all \(J_i\).
Rank 1 (\(k=1\)): A vector operator, e.g., the position operator \(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\) or the electric dipole operator. The spherical components are \(T^{(1)}_0 = z\) and \(T^{(1)}_{\pm 1} = \mp(x \pm iy)/\sqrt{2}\).
Rank 2 (\(k=2\)): The electric quadrupole moment. Its five components are formed from the symmetric traceless combinations of the position coordinates.



Statement of the theorem
The Wigner-Eckart theorem states that the matrix element of a spherical tensor operator between angular momentum eigenstates takes the factored form \[
\langle j', m' | T^{(k)}_q | j, m \rangle = \langle j, m; k, q | j', m' \rangle \; \langle j' \| T^{(k)} \| j \rangle.
\]
Here \(\langle j, m; k, q | j', m' \rangle\) is a Clebsch-Gordan coefficient and \(\langle j' \| T^{(k)} \| j \rangle\) is the reduced matrix element. The key point is:

The reduced matrix element \(\langle j' \| T^{(k)} \| j \rangle\) is independent of \(m\), \(m'\), and \(q\).

All dependence on the magnetic quantum numbers is carried entirely by the Clebsch-Gordan coefficient, which is a purely kinematic quantity determined by the geometry of angular momentum coupling. The reduced matrix element encodes the dynamical information specific to the physical system — the radial wavefunctions, the interaction strength, and so forth.


Physical consequences
Separation of geometry from dynamics. The theorem tells us that among the \((2j+1)(2k+1)\) matrix elements \(\langle j', m' | T^{(k)}_q | j, m \rangle\) (for fixed \(j\), \(j'\), and \(k\) but varying \(m\), \(m'\), \(q\)), all are proportional to a single number: the reduced matrix element. The relative magnitudes of different matrix elements are fixed by group theory alone. Only the overall scale requires a dynamical calculation.
Selection rules. The Clebsch-Gordan coefficient \(\langle j, m; k, q | j', m' \rangle\) vanishes unless two conditions are met:

Magnetic selection rule: \(m' = m + q\), i.e., \(\Delta m = q\).
Triangle rule: \(|j - k| \leq j' \leq j + k\).

If either condition fails, the matrix element is exactly zero regardless of the dynamics. These selection rules are a direct consequence of the representation theory of \(SU(2)\).


Example: electric dipole transitions in hydrogen
The electric dipole operator is the position vector \(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\), which is a rank-1 spherical tensor: \(\hat{\mathbf{r}} \sim T^{(1)}\). The transition amplitude for a photon-induced transition between hydrogen states \(|n, \ell, m\rangle\) and \(|n', \ell', m'\rangle\) is proportional to \[
\langle n', \ell', m' | T^{(1)}_q | n, \ell, m \rangle = \langle \ell, m; 1, q | \ell', m' \rangle \; \langle n', \ell' \| T^{(1)} \| n, \ell \rangle.
\]
The triangle rule for \(k = 1\) requires \(|\ell - 1| \leq \ell' \leq \ell + 1\), which gives the celebrated electric dipole selection rule \(\Delta \ell = 0, \pm 1\). However, the case \(\Delta \ell = 0\) is further excluded by parity (since \(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\) is odd under parity and the parity of \(|n, \ell, m\rangle\) is \((-1)^\ell\)), leaving \[
\Delta \ell = \pm 1, \qquad \Delta m = 0, \pm 1.
\]
The reduced matrix element \(\langle n', \ell' \| T^{(1)} \| n, \ell \rangle\) involves the radial integral \(\int_0^\infty R_{n'\ell'}(r) \, r \, R_{n\ell}(r) \, r^2 \, dr\), which must be computed from the hydrogen wavefunctions. But the selection rules on \(\ell\) and \(m\) — which dictate which transitions are allowed at all — follow from the Wigner-Eckart theorem without any knowledge of the radial wavefunctions.

title: Group Theory in Quantum Mechanics
text:
Selection Rules from Symmetry
The Wigner-Eckart theorem provides selection rules for angular momentum. But the idea of deriving selection rules from representation theory is far more general and applies to any symmetry group.

The general principle
Consider a matrix element \(\langle f | \hat{O} | i \rangle\), where \(|i\rangle\) transforms as an irrep \(\Gamma_i\) of a symmetry group \(G\), \(|f\rangle\) transforms as \(\Gamma_f\), and the operator \(\hat{O}\) transforms as \(\Gamma_O\). The integrand (more precisely, the quantity whose expectation value we compute) transforms as the tensor product representation \[
\Gamma_f^* \otimes \Gamma_O \otimes \Gamma_i.
\]
The matrix element vanishes unless this tensor product contains the trivial (identity) representation \(\Gamma_0\) of \(G\): \[
\langle f | \hat{O} | i \rangle = 0 \quad \text{unless} \quad \Gamma_0 \subseteq \Gamma_f^* \otimes \Gamma_O \otimes \Gamma_i.
\]
Equivalently, \(\langle f | \hat{O} | i \rangle\) can be nonzero only if \(\Gamma_f\) appears in the decomposition of \(\Gamma_O \otimes \Gamma_i\). This is the master selection rule of representation theory. All concrete selection rules (for angular momentum, parity, crystal symmetry, and so on) are special cases.
The reasoning is straightforward: if the integrand transforms nontrivially under some symmetry of the system, then the integral is mapped to a multiple of itself by that symmetry transformation. If the representation has no trivial component, the only consistent value for the integral is zero.


Parity selection rules
Parity is the simplest example beyond angular momentum. The parity group \(\mathbb{Z}_2 = \{e, P\}\) has two irreps: the even representation $_+ $ (with \(P \to +1\)) and the odd representation \(\Gamma_-\) (with \(P \to -1\)).
An operator \(\hat{O}\) has definite parity: \(P \hat{O} P^{-1} = \pm \hat{O}\). Then \(\hat{O}\) transforms as \(\Gamma_+\) if it is even (a scalar or pseudovector under parity) or as \(\Gamma_-\) if it is odd (a polar vector).
The tensor product rule for \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) is simply the multiplication of signs: \(\Gamma_+ \otimes \Gamma_+ = \Gamma_+\), \(\Gamma_+ \otimes \Gamma_- = \Gamma_-\), \(\Gamma_- \otimes \Gamma_- = \Gamma_+\). The matrix element \(\langle f | \hat{O} | i \rangle\) is nonzero only if \(\Gamma_f^* \otimes \Gamma_O \otimes \Gamma_i = \Gamma_+\) (the trivial representation). Since all irreps of \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) are real, \(\Gamma_f^* = \Gamma_f\). Therefore:

If \(\hat{O}\) is even (\(\Gamma_O = \Gamma_+\)): the matrix element is nonzero only if \(|i\rangle\) and \(|f\rangle\) have the same parity.
If \(\hat{O}\) is odd (\(\Gamma_O = \Gamma_-\)): the matrix element is nonzero only if \(|i\rangle\) and \(|f\rangle\) have opposite parity.

For the electric dipole operator \(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\), which is odd under parity, this immediately gives the parity selection rule: electric dipole transitions connect states of opposite parity. In atomic physics, this means \(\Delta \ell = \text{odd}\), which (combined with the angular momentum triangle rule) restricts us to \(\Delta \ell = \pm 1\).


Combining selection rules
In practice, multiple symmetries act simultaneously, and the matrix element must satisfy the selection rules from each symmetry independently. For a rotationally invariant system with parity, the full selection rule for electric dipole transitions is:

From \(SU(2)\): \(|j - 1| \leq j' \leq j + 1\) and \(\Delta m = q\).
From parity: \((-1)^{\ell'} = -(-1)^{\ell}\), i.e., \(\Delta \ell = \text{odd}\).

The intersection of these constraints gives the complete selection rule. The power of the representation-theoretic approach is that it reduces the question “which transitions are allowed?” to a problem of decomposing tensor products of representations — a purely algebraic computation that requires no knowledge of wavefunctions or matrix elements.

title: Group Theory in Quantum Mechanics
text:
Character Theory

Characters as class functions
The character of a representation \(D\) evaluated at \(g \in G\) is the trace: \[
\chi_D(g) = \mathrm{Tr}[D(g)].
\]
Characters are class functions: they depend only on the conjugacy class of \(g\), since \(\mathrm{Tr}[D(hgh^{-1})] = \mathrm{Tr}[D(g)]\). Two representations are equivalent if and only if they have the same character.


Orthogonality relations
For a finite group \(G\), the characters of irreps satisfy the great orthogonality theorem: \[
\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G} \chi_\alpha(g)^* \, \chi_\beta(g) = \delta_{\alpha\beta},
\] where \(\alpha, \beta\) label irreps. This is an orthonormality relation on the space of class functions, with the inner product \(\langle f_1, f_2\rangle = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_g f_1(g)^* f_2(g)\).
The number of distinct irreps equals the number of conjugacy classes. Their dimensions \(d_\alpha\) satisfy \[
\sum_\alpha d_\alpha^2 = |G|.
\]
Example: \(\mathbb{Z}_3\). The group \(\mathbb{Z}_3 = \{e, r, r^2\}\) (with \(r^3 = e\)) has three conjugacy classes (each element is its own class, since the group is abelian) and three one-dimensional irreps. Setting \(\omega = e^{2\pi i/3}\), the characters are:

The orthogonality relations are easily verified. The decomposition formula tells us how many times irrep \(\alpha\) appears in a given representation: \(n_\alpha = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_g \chi_\alpha(g)^* \chi(g)\).


Character table for \(S_3\)
A more substantial example is the symmetric group \(S_3\) on three objects, which is isomorphic to the point group \(C_{3v}\) (the symmetry group of an equilateral triangle). This is the smallest non-abelian group and has order \(|S_3| = 6\).
Conjugacy classes. The six elements fall into three conjugacy classes:

\(\{e\}\): the identity (1 element).
\(\{(123), (132)\}\): the two 3-cycles, i.e., rotations by \(120°\) and \(240°\) (2 elements).
\(\{(12), (13), (23)\}\): the three transpositions, i.e., reflections (3 elements).

Since there are three conjugacy classes, there are exactly three irreducible representations. Their dimensions \(d_1, d_2, d_3\) must satisfy \(d_1^2 + d_2^2 + d_3^2 = 6\), which has the unique solution (up to ordering) \(d_1 = 1, d_2 = 1, d_3 = 2\).
The three irreps are:

\(\Gamma_{\text{triv}}\) (dimension 1): the trivial representation, where every element maps to \(+1\).
\(\Gamma_{\text{sign}}\) (dimension 1): the sign (alternating) representation, where even permutations map to \(+1\) and odd permutations map to \(-1\).
\(\Gamma_{\text{std}}\) (dimension 2): the standard representation, obtained from the natural 3-dimensional permutation representation by restricting to the 2-dimensional subspace orthogonal to the vector \((1, 1, 1)\).

The complete character table is:

Verifying orthogonality. The orthogonality relation \(\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_C |C| \, \chi_\alpha(C)^* \chi_\beta(C) = \delta_{\alpha\beta}\) can be checked explicitly. For example, taking \(\alpha = \Gamma_{\text{sign}}\) and \(\beta = \Gamma_{\text{std}}\): \[
\frac{1}{6}\left[1 \cdot 1 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 1 \cdot (-1) + 3 \cdot (-1) \cdot 0\right] = \frac{1}{6}(2 - 2 + 0) = 0. \quad \checkmark
\]
Decomposing a representation. Suppose we have a 6-dimensional representation whose character is \(\chi(e) = 6\), \(\chi(123) = 0\), \(\chi(12) = 2\). The multiplicity of each irrep is: \[
n_{\text{triv}} = \frac{1}{6}(1 \cdot 6 + 2 \cdot 0 + 3 \cdot 2) = 2,
\] \[
n_{\text{sign}} = \frac{1}{6}(1 \cdot 6 + 2 \cdot 0 + 3 \cdot (-1) \cdot 2) = 0,
\] \[
n_{\text{std}} = \frac{1}{6}(1 \cdot 2 \cdot 6 + 2 \cdot (-1) \cdot 0 + 3 \cdot 0 \cdot 2) = 2.
\] So the representation decomposes as \(2\,\Gamma_{\text{triv}} \oplus 2\,\Gamma_{\text{std}}\), with total dimension \(2 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 2 = 6\). \(\checkmark\)
This procedure — computing multiplicities via the decomposition formula using the character table — works for any finite group representation and is the standard method for predicting how energy levels split when symmetry is reduced.

title: Group Theory in Quantum Mechanics
text:
Worked Examples

The hydrogen atom: SO(3) and accidental SO(4) symmetry
The Coulomb Hamiltonian \[
H = \frac{\mathbf{p}^2}{2m} - \frac{e^2}{r}
\] is invariant under \(SO(3)\) rotations. Therefore, by the representation theory of \(SO(3)\), each energy level must form an irrep (or direct sum of irreps) of \(SO(3)\). The angular momentum quantum number \(\ell\) labels the irrep, and states with a given \(\ell\) are \((2\ell+1)\)-fold degenerate.
But the hydrogen atom has a larger degeneracy than \(SO(3)\) alone requires. For principal quantum number \(n\), the states with \(\ell = 0, 1, \ldots, n-1\) are all degenerate, giving a total degeneracy of \(n^2\) (ignoring spin). This is not explained by rotational symmetry — it is an accidental degeneracy arising from a hidden SO(4) symmetry.
The additional symmetry is generated by the Laplace–Runge–Lenz vector \[
\mathbf{A} = \frac{1}{2m}(\mathbf{p} \times \mathbf{L} - \mathbf{L} \times \mathbf{p}) - \frac{e^2 \mathbf{r}}{r},
\] which satisfies \([H, \mathbf{A}] = 0\). Together with \(\mathbf{L}\), the components of \(\mathbf{A}\) (suitably normalized on a fixed energy shell) generate an \(\mathfrak{so}(4) \cong \mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{su}(2)\) algebra. The bound states at energy \(E_n\) transform as the \((j, j)\) representation of \(SU(2) \times SU(2)\) with \(j = (n-1)/2\), which has dimension \((2j+1)^2 = n^2\). This completely explains the observed degeneracy.
This is a beautiful example of how group theory reveals hidden structure: the “accidental” degeneracy is not accidental at all, but a consequence of an enhanced symmetry specific to the \(1/r\) potential.


The harmonic oscillator: SU(N) symmetry
The \(N\)-dimensional isotropic harmonic oscillator \[
H = \frac{\mathbf{p}^2}{2m} + \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 \mathbf{r}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\hbar\omega\left(a_i^\dagger a_i + \frac{1}{2}\right)
\] has energy levels \(E_n = \hbar\omega(n + N/2)\). The degeneracy of the \(n\)-th level is \(\binom{n+N-1}{N-1}\), which grows as a polynomial in \(n\).
The symmetry group is \(SU(N)\). The generators are the \(N^2 - 1\) bilinear operators \(a_i^\dagger a_j - \frac{1}{N}\delta_{ij}\hat{n}\) (traceless combinations), which all commute with \(H\). The states at level \(n\) transform as the completely symmetric representation of \(SU(N)\) with \(n\) indices, which has dimension \(\binom{n+N-1}{N-1}\).
For \(N = 3\), this is \(SU(3)\), and the level-\(n\) degeneracy is \(\frac{1}{2}(n+1)(n+2)\): 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, \(\ldots\) The decomposition under the \(SO(3)\) subgroup gives \(\ell = n, n-2, n-4, \ldots, 0 \text{ or } 1\), recovering the familiar angular momentum content.


Crystal field splitting: branching rules from \(SO(3)\) to \(O_h\)
When an atom is placed in a crystal, the full \(SO(3)\) rotational symmetry is broken to the point group \(G\) of the crystal site. An atomic level that transformed as an irrep of \(SO(3)\) with angular momentum \(\ell\) (and degeneracy \(2\ell+1\)) now splits into irreps of \(G\).
The splitting is determined by restricting the \(SO(3)\) representation to \(G\) and decomposing it into irreps of \(G\). This is called subduction or branching. The tool for computing these branching rules is the character: we evaluate the \(SO(3)\) character \(\chi^{(\ell)}(\theta) = \frac{\sin((2\ell+1)\theta/2)}{\sin(\theta/2)}\) on the conjugacy classes of \(G\), then use the decomposition formula with the character table of \(G\).
The octahedral group \(O_h\). The full octahedral group \(O_h = O \times \{e, i\}\) includes inversions. The proper rotation subgroup \(O\) has order 24, with five conjugacy classes: \(\{e\}\), \(\{6C_4\}\) (rotations by \(\pm 90°\) about cube axes), \(\{3C_4^2 = 3C_2\}\) (rotations by \(180°\) about cube axes), \(\{8C_3\}\) (rotations by \(\pm 120°\) about body diagonals), and \(\{6C_2'\}\) (rotations by \(180°\) about face diagonals). Including inversion doubles the group to order 48 and introduces the gerade (\(g\)) and ungerade (\(u\)) labels.
The irreps of \(O\) (and their dimensions) are: \(A_1\) (1), \(A_2\) (1), \(E\) (2), \(T_1\) (3), \(T_2\) (3). With inversion, each acquires a \(g/u\) subscript.
Branching rules for \(\ell = 0, 1, 2, 3\):
For \(\ell = 0\) (\(s\)-orbital, dimension 1): The \(SO(3)\) character is \(\chi^{(0)} = 1\) for all rotations. The only matching irrep of \(O_h\) is the trivial representation: \[
D^{(0)} \downarrow O_h = A_{1g}.
\] The \(s\)-orbital is unsplit, as expected — it is a singlet.
For \(\ell = 1\) (\(p\)-orbital, dimension 3): The character values are \(\chi^{(1)}(e) = 3\), \(\chi^{(1)}(C_4) = 1\), \(\chi^{(1)}(C_2) = -1\), \(\chi^{(1)}(C_3) = 0\), \(\chi^{(1)}(C_2') = -1\). Comparing with the \(O\) character table, this matches \(T_1\) exactly. Since \(p\)-orbitals are odd under parity (\((-1)^\ell = -1\)): \[
D^{(1)} \downarrow O_h = T_{1u}.
\] The \(p\)-orbital remains unsplit in an octahedral field — the three \(p\)-orbitals transform as a single irreducible triplet.
For \(\ell = 2\) (\(d\)-orbital, dimension 5): The character values are \(\chi^{(2)}(e) = 5\), \(\chi^{(2)}(C_4) = -1\), \(\chi^{(2)}(C_2) = 1\), \(\chi^{(2)}(C_3) = -1\), \(\chi^{(2)}(C_2') = 1\). Applying the decomposition formula: \[
D^{(2)} \downarrow O_h = E_g \oplus T_{2g},
\] where \(E_g\) is 2-dimensional and \(T_{2g}\) is 3-dimensional (\(2 + 3 = 5\)). This is the famous \(e_g\)–\(t_{2g}\) splitting of crystal field theory.
Physically, the \(e_g\) orbitals are \(d_{z^2}\) and \(d_{x^2-y^2}\), which point directly toward the six ligands along the coordinate axes in an octahedral complex. The \(t_{2g}\) orbitals are \(d_{xy}\), \(d_{xz}\), and \(d_{yz}\), which point between the ligands. The electrostatic repulsion from the ligands raises the energy of the \(e_g\) orbitals relative to \(t_{2g}\). The energy splitting \(\Delta_{\text{oct}} = 10Dq\) depends on the ligand field strength, but the pattern of splitting into a doublet and a triplet is dictated purely by group theory.
For \(\ell = 3\) (\(f\)-orbital, dimension 7): The character values are \(\chi^{(3)}(e) = 7\), \(\chi^{(3)}(C_4) = -1\), \(\chi^{(3)}(C_2) = -1\), \(\chi^{(3)}(C_3) = 1\), \(\chi^{(3)}(C_2') = 1\). Decomposing: \[
D^{(3)} \downarrow O_h = A_{2u} \oplus T_{1u} \oplus T_{2u},
\] giving \(1 + 3 + 3 = 7\). The \(f\)-shell splits into a singlet and two triplets.

These branching rules are computed using the character tables of \(O_h\) and the decomposition formula. They are tabulated in standard references and are essential tools in spectroscopy, transition metal chemistry, and condensed matter physics. The \(e_g\)–\(t_{2g}\) splitting of \(d\)-orbitals, in particular, governs the electronic structure and magnetic properties of transition metal complexes: it determines the crystal field stabilization energy, controls whether a complex is high-spin or low-spin, and explains the colors of coordination compounds through \(d\)–\(d\) transitions.

title: Group Theory in Quantum Mechanics
text:
Point Groups and Space Groups

Point groups
A point group is a finite subgroup of \(O(3)\) that leaves at least one point fixed. The crystallographic point groups — those compatible with a lattice — number 32 in three dimensions. They are classified as:

Cyclic groups \(C_n\): \(n\)-fold rotation axis.
Dihedral groups \(D_n\): \(n\)-fold axis plus \(n\) perpendicular 2-fold axes.
Cubic groups \(T\), \(O\), \(T_d\), \(T_h\), \(O_h\): the symmetries of the tetrahedron and octahedron/cube.
Various extensions with improper rotations (reflections, inversions).

The representation theory of these finite groups is well-developed: each has a finite character table, and all irreps can be explicitly constructed. The branching rules from \(SO(3)\) to any point group are tabulated and allow immediate prediction of crystal field splittings.


Beyond point groups: space groups and band theory
In a periodic solid, the full symmetry is a space group: a point group combined with translations. The representation theory of space groups leads to Bloch’s theorem (states are labeled by crystal momentum \(\mathbf{k}\)) and the classification of band structures. The irreps of the little group at each high-symmetry point in the Brillouin zone determine the allowed band degeneracies and crossings. This is the group-theoretic foundation of topological band theory.

title: Group Theory in Quantum Mechanics
text:
Summary
The key takeaways:

Symmetries of \(H\) organize the spectrum. If \([H, D(g)] = 0\) for all \(g \in G\), energy eigenspaces carry representations of \(G\).
Schur’s lemma implies degeneracy. Irreducible representations cannot be split by any operator commuting with \(G\), so the dimension of the irrep is a lower bound on the degeneracy.
\(SU(2)\) irreps are labeled by \(j\) with dimension \(2j+1\). This explains the \(2\ell+1\) degeneracy of angular momentum multiplets and the rules for adding angular momenta.
The Wigner-Eckart theorem factorizes matrix elements into geometry (Clebsch-Gordan coefficients) and dynamics (reduced matrix elements), yielding selection rules from representation theory alone.
Selection rules from symmetry follow from the general principle: \(\langle f | \hat{O} | i \rangle = 0\) unless \(\Gamma_f^* \otimes \Gamma_O \otimes \Gamma_i\) contains the trivial representation. This unifies angular momentum and parity selection rules.
Accidental degeneracies signal hidden symmetries: \(SO(4)\) in hydrogen, \(SU(N)\) in the isotropic oscillator.
Symmetry breaking (e.g., by a crystal field) splits multiplets according to branching rules that are determined entirely by the group-subgroup relationship. The \(e_g\)–\(t_{2g}\) splitting of \(d\)-orbitals in an octahedral field is a prime example.

title: Quantum Information and Computation
text:
Quantum information theory asks a deceptively simple question: what can you do with quantum states that you cannot do with classical bits? The answer turns out to reshape our understanding of computation, communication, and even the structure of spacetime. These notes collect the core results that any working physicist should have at their fingertips — the no-cloning theorem, the limits of state discrimination, the structure of entanglement, and the formalism of quantum channels — before sketching how these ideas connect to tensor network methods and holography.
Throughout, we work with finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces \(\mathcal{H} \cong \mathbb{C}^d\) unless otherwise stated, and we set \(\hbar = 1\).

Throughout, we work with finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces \(\mathcal{H} \cong \mathbb{C}^d\) unless otherwise stated, and we set \(\hbar = 1\).

title: Quantum Information and Computation
text:
The No-Cloning Theorem

Statement
The no-cloning theorem is one of the earliest and most consequential results in quantum information. It asserts that there is no physical process that can duplicate an arbitrary unknown quantum state.
Theorem (Wootters–Zurek, Dieks, 1982). There exists no unitary operator \(U\) acting on \(\mathcal{H} \otimes \mathcal{H}\) such that, for every state \(|\psi\rangle \in \mathcal{H}\), \[
U \bigl(|\psi\rangle \otimes |0\rangle\bigr) = |\psi\rangle \otimes |\psi\rangle,
\] where \(|0\rangle\) is some fixed blank state.


Proof
The proof is short and uses only two properties of quantum mechanics: linearity and the preservation of inner products by unitary evolution.
Suppose such a \(U\) exists. Take two states \(|\psi\rangle\) and \(|\phi\rangle\), and assume the cloning relation holds for both: \[
U(|\psi\rangle \otimes |0\rangle) = |\psi\rangle \otimes |\psi\rangle, \qquad U(|\phi\rangle \otimes |0\rangle) = |\phi\rangle \otimes |\phi\rangle.
\]
Since \(U\) is unitary, it preserves inner products. Compute the overlap of the left-hand sides: \[
\bigl(\langle\psi| \otimes \langle 0|\bigr)\bigl(|\phi\rangle \otimes |0\rangle\bigr) = \langle\psi|\phi\rangle \cdot \langle 0|0\rangle = \langle\psi|\phi\rangle.
\]
Now compute the overlap of the right-hand sides: \[
\bigl(\langle\psi| \otimes \langle\psi|\bigr)\bigl(|\phi\rangle \otimes |\phi\rangle\bigr) = \langle\psi|\phi\rangle^2.
\]
Equating, we need \[
\langle\psi|\phi\rangle = \langle\psi|\phi\rangle^2,
\] which forces \(\langle\psi|\phi\rangle \in \{0, 1\}\). So the cloning machine can only work if the two states are either identical or orthogonal — it cannot clone a pair of non-orthogonal states. Since a universal cloner must handle arbitrary states, no such \(U\) exists. \(\blacksquare\)


Physical implications
The no-cloning theorem is not merely a mathematical curiosity. It has profound physical consequences:

Quantum key distribution. The security of protocols like BB84 rests on no-cloning: an eavesdropper cannot copy the transmitted quantum states without disturbing them, and this disturbance is detectable.
Quantum error correction. Since we cannot copy quantum states, error correction in the quantum setting requires a fundamentally different approach from classical repetition codes. The trick is to encode information in entangled states across multiple qubits without ever learning (and thus collapsing) the logical state.
No superluminal signalling. If cloning were possible, one could use it together with entanglement to send information faster than light. The no-cloning theorem is thus intimately connected to relativistic causality.



Approximate cloning
While perfect cloning is impossible, one can ask: how well can we clone? The optimal approximate cloner for qubits was found by Buzek and Hillery (1996). For a \(1 \to 2\) symmetric cloner acting on qubits, the optimal single-copy fidelity is \[
F = \frac{5}{6} \approx 0.833.
\]
More generally, for a \(1 \to M\) cloner in dimension \(d\), the optimal fidelity is \[
F = \frac{M(d-1) + d + M}{M(d+1)}.
\]
These bounds are tight and can be achieved by specific quantum circuits. The existence of a gap between the cloning fidelity and unity is another way of quantifying the “quantumness” of information.


The no-deleting theorem
The no-cloning theorem has a natural complement: the no-deleting theorem (Pati and Braunstein, 2000). While no-cloning says you cannot create a copy of an unknown quantum state, no-deleting says you cannot destroy one of two copies of an unknown state against a blank ancilla while keeping the other intact.
Theorem. There exists no linear operator \(U\) acting on \(\mathcal{H} \otimes \mathcal{H} \otimes \mathcal{H}_A\) such that, for every \(|\psi\rangle\), \[
U\bigl(|\psi\rangle \otimes |\psi\rangle \otimes |A\rangle\bigr) = |\psi\rangle \otimes |0\rangle \otimes |A'\rangle,
\] where \(|0\rangle\) is a fixed state and \(|A'\rangle\) may depend on \(|\psi\rangle\).
The proof strategy mirrors that of no-cloning. If such a \(U\) existed, taking two input states \(|\psi\rangle\) and \(|\phi\rangle\) and computing inner products of both sides yields \[
\langle\psi|\phi\rangle^2 \langle A|A\rangle = \langle\psi|\phi\rangle \langle 0|0\rangle \langle A'_\psi|A'_\phi\rangle,
\] which simplifies to \(\langle\psi|\phi\rangle = \langle A'_\psi|A'_\phi\rangle\). This means the “deleted” information has been transferred entirely into the ancilla, not destroyed — quantum information is never lost, only moved. This is a direct manifestation of unitarity: since quantum time evolution is reversible, information can be scrambled or redistributed but never erased.
Together, no-cloning and no-deleting express a deep principle: quantum information is conserved. You can move it, encode it, spread it across entangled subsystems, but you can neither duplicate it nor annihilate it. This conservation law is closely related to the unitarity of quantum mechanics and has direct implications for the black hole information paradox, where the question is precisely whether information thrown into a black hole is truly destroyed or eventually recovered.

title: Quantum Information and Computation
text:
Quantum State Discrimination

The problem
Suppose Alice prepares one of two quantum states \(\rho_1\) or \(\rho_2\) with prior probabilities \(p_1\) and \(p_2 = 1 - p_1\), and sends it to Bob. Bob must perform a measurement and guess which state was sent. If \(\rho_1\) and \(\rho_2\) are orthogonal, Bob can distinguish them perfectly. But if they are non-orthogonal, errors are unavoidable. The question is: what is the minimum probability of error?


Minimum error discrimination: the Helstrom bound
The optimal strategy is described by a two-outcome POVM \(\{E_1, E_2\}\) with \(E_1 + E_2 = \mathbb{I}\), \(E_i \geq 0\). The probability of error is \[
P_{\rm err} = p_1 \, \mathrm{Tr}(\rho_1 E_2) + p_2 \, \mathrm{Tr}(\rho_2 E_1).
\]
Theorem (Helstrom, 1976). The minimum error probability for discriminating between \(\rho_1\) and \(\rho_2\) with priors \(p_1, p_2\) is \[
P_{\rm err} = \frac{1}{2}\bigl(1 - \|p_1 \rho_1 - p_2 \rho_2\|_1\bigr),
\] where \(\|A\|_1 = \mathrm{Tr}\sqrt{A^\dagger A}\) is the trace norm.
The optimal POVM is obtained by diagonalizing \(\Lambda = p_1 \rho_1 - p_2 \rho_2\) and assigning \(E_1\) to the positive eigenspace and \(E_2\) to the negative eigenspace.
Example: two pure qubit states. For \(|\psi_1\rangle\) and \(|\psi_2\rangle\) with equal priors (\(p_1 = p_2 = 1/2\)) and overlap \(|\langle\psi_1|\psi_2\rangle| = \cos\theta\), the Helstrom bound gives \[
P_{\rm err} = \frac{1}{2}(1 - \sin\theta).
\]
When \(\theta = \pi/2\) (orthogonal states), we get \(P_{\rm err} = 0\). When \(\theta = 0\) (identical states), \(P_{\rm err} = 1/2\) — pure guessing. Everything in between interpolates smoothly.


Unambiguous discrimination
An alternative strategy is unambiguous state discrimination (USD): Bob is allowed to sometimes output “I don’t know,” but when he does give an answer, it must be correct with certainty. For two pure states with equal priors, the optimal failure probability (the probability of the inconclusive outcome) is \[
P_{\rm fail} = |\langle\psi_1|\psi_2\rangle|.
\]
This was first derived by Ivanovic (1987), Dieks (1988), and Peres (1988). USD is only possible when the states have linearly independent support; for two states with overlapping support (mixed states whose supports are not orthogonal), unambiguous discrimination may be impossible.


Relation to no-cloning
State discrimination and no-cloning are deeply connected. If we could clone, we could make many copies of the unknown state and perform tomography, distinguishing any two states with arbitrarily small error. The Helstrom bound is thus a quantitative expression of the same physics that forbids cloning.


Worked example: discriminating \(|0\rangle\) and a rotated state
Consider the concrete problem of discriminating \(|\psi_1\rangle = |0\rangle\) and \(|\psi_2\rangle = \cos\theta\,|0\rangle + \sin\theta\,|1\rangle\) with equal priors \(p_1 = p_2 = 1/2\). We compute the Helstrom bound and the optimal measurement explicitly.
Step 1: form the Helstrom operator. Define \(\Lambda = p_1|\psi_1\rangle\langle\psi_1| - p_2|\psi_2\rangle\langle\psi_2|\). In the \(\{|0\rangle, |1\rangle\}\) basis: \[
\Lambda = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} - \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta \\ \sin\theta \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 - \cos^2\theta & -\cos\theta\sin\theta \\ -\cos\theta\sin\theta & -\sin^2\theta \end{pmatrix}.
\] Using \(1 - \cos^2\theta = \sin^2\theta\), this simplifies to \[
\Lambda = \frac{\sin\theta}{2}\begin{pmatrix} \sin\theta & -\cos\theta \\ -\cos\theta & -\sin\theta \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Step 2: diagonalize \(\Lambda\). The matrix in parentheses has eigenvalues \(\pm 1\) (it is traceless with determinant \(-\sin^2\theta - \cos^2\theta = -1\)), so the eigenvalues of \(\Lambda\) are \(\pm \frac{\sin\theta}{2}\). The trace norm is therefore \[
\|\Lambda\|_1 = \frac{\sin\theta}{2} + \frac{\sin\theta}{2} = \sin\theta.
\]
Step 3: the Helstrom bound. The minimum error probability is \[
P_{\rm err} = \frac{1}{2}(1 - \sin\theta),
\] matching the general formula for two pure states with overlap \(|\langle\psi_1|\psi_2\rangle| = \cos\theta\).
Step 4: the optimal POVM. The eigenvector of \(\Lambda\) with positive eigenvalue \(+\frac{\sin\theta}{2}\) is \[
|v_+\rangle = \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\,|0\rangle - \sin\frac{\theta}{2}\,|1\rangle,
\] and the eigenvector with negative eigenvalue is \[
|v_-\rangle = \sin\frac{\theta}{2}\,|0\rangle + \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\,|1\rangle.
\] The optimal POVM is the projective measurement in this basis: \(E_1 = |v_+\rangle\langle v_+|\) (guess \(\psi_1\)) and \(E_2 = |v_-\rangle\langle v_-|\) (guess \(\psi_2\)). Note that the measurement basis lies along the angle bisector of the two states on the Bloch sphere — this is geometrically intuitive, as the optimal discriminator should be oriented to maximally separate the two signal states.
As a check: when \(\theta = \pi/4\), the states \(|0\rangle\) and \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|0\rangle + |1\rangle)\) give \(P_{\rm err} = \frac{1}{2}(1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}) \approx 0.146\), and the measurement is performed in the basis tilted at \(\pi/8\) from the computational basis.

title: Quantum Information and Computation
text:
Entanglement

Bell states
The maximally entangled states of two qubits are the Bell states: \[
|\Phi^+\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|00\rangle + |11\rangle), \qquad |\Phi^-\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|00\rangle - |11\rangle),
\] \[
|\Psi^+\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|01\rangle + |10\rangle), \qquad |\Psi^-\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|01\rangle - |10\rangle).
\]
These form an orthonormal basis for \(\mathbb{C}^2 \otimes \mathbb{C}^2\). Any of the four can be obtained from any other by a local unitary on one qubit. The reduced density matrix of each Bell state is \(\rho_A = \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{I}\) — maximally mixed.


Schmidt decomposition
Any bipartite pure state \(|\psi\rangle \in \mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B\) can be written as \[
|\psi\rangle = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \lambda_i \, |a_i\rangle \otimes |b_i\rangle,
\] where \(\{|a_i\rangle\}\) and \(\{|b_i\rangle\}\) are orthonormal sets in \(\mathcal{H}_A\) and \(\mathcal{H}_B\) respectively, \(\lambda_i > 0\), and \(\sum_i \lambda_i^2 = 1\). The number \(r\) is the Schmidt rank, and the \(\lambda_i\) are the Schmidt coefficients.
The Schmidt decomposition is simply the singular value decomposition (SVD) applied to the coefficient matrix \(C_{ij}\) in any product basis expansion \(|\psi\rangle = \sum_{ij} C_{ij} |i\rangle|j\rangle\). A state is entangled if and only if its Schmidt rank is greater than 1.


Von Neumann entropy as an entanglement measure
For a bipartite pure state \(|\psi\rangle_{AB}\) with reduced density matrix \(\rho_A = \mathrm{Tr}_B(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\), the entanglement entropy is the von Neumann entropy of the reduced state: \[
S(\rho_A) = -\mathrm{Tr}(\rho_A \log \rho_A) = -\sum_i \lambda_i^2 \log \lambda_i^2,
\] where \(\lambda_i\) are the Schmidt coefficients. This is the unique measure of bipartite pure-state entanglement (up to normalization) satisfying natural axioms: it vanishes for product states, is maximized for maximally entangled states, and does not increase under local operations and classical communication (LOCC).
For a maximally entangled state of two \(d\)-dimensional systems, \(S = \log d\).


Entanglement of formation
For mixed states, quantifying entanglement is harder. The entanglement of formation \(E_F(\rho)\) is defined as the minimum average entanglement over all pure-state decompositions: \[
E_F(\rho) = \min_{\{p_i, |\psi_i\rangle\}} \sum_i p_i \, S(\mathrm{Tr}_B |\psi_i\rangle\langle\psi_i|),
\] where the minimum is over all ensembles \(\{p_i, |\psi_i\rangle\}\) such that \(\rho = \sum_i p_i |\psi_i\rangle\langle\psi_i|\).
For two qubits, Wootters (1998) found an elegant closed-form expression for \(E_F\) in terms of the concurrence \(C(\rho)\): \[
E_F = h\!\left(\frac{1 + \sqrt{1-C^2}}{2}\right),
\] where \(h(x) = -x\log x - (1-x)\log(1-x)\) is the binary entropy. The concurrence can be computed from the eigenvalues of \(\rho(\sigma_y \otimes \sigma_y)\rho^*(\sigma_y \otimes \sigma_y)\).


Monogamy of entanglement
Entanglement is monogamous: if qubit \(A\) is maximally entangled with qubit \(B\), it cannot be entangled with a third qubit \(C\) at all. Quantitatively, the Coffman–Kundu–Wootters (CKW) inequality states that for three qubits, \[
C^2_{A|BC} \geq C^2_{AB} + C^2_{AC},
\] where \(C_{AB}\) is the concurrence of the reduced state \(\rho_{AB}\), and \(C_{A|BC}\) is the concurrence between \(A\) and the joint system \(BC\).
Monogamy is a distinctly quantum phenomenon with no classical analogue — classical correlations can be freely shared. It plays a central role in the security proofs of quantum key distribution and, remarkably, also appears in black hole physics through the “monogamy vs. ER=EPR” discussion.


Quantum teleportation
Quantum teleportation (Bennett et al., 1993) is the protocol that most vividly demonstrates the power of entanglement as a resource. It allows Alice to transmit an unknown qubit state \(|\psi\rangle = \alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle\) to Bob using one shared Bell pair and two classical bits — without any quantum channel between them at the time of transmission.
Setup. Alice and Bob share the Bell state \(|\Phi^+\rangle_{AB} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|00\rangle + |11\rangle)_{AB}\). Alice also holds the state \(|\psi\rangle_Q\) she wishes to teleport. The total initial state of the three qubits \(Q\), \(A\), \(B\) is \[
|\Psi_0\rangle = |\psi\rangle_Q \otimes |\Phi^+\rangle_{AB} = (\alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle)_Q \otimes \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|00\rangle + |11\rangle)_{AB}.
\]
Step 1: rewrite in the Bell basis. The key algebraic identity is the expansion of a product basis in terms of Bell states. For any two qubits \(Q\) and \(A\): \[
|0\rangle_Q|0\rangle_A = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|\Phi^+\rangle + |\Phi^-\rangle), \qquad |0\rangle_Q|1\rangle_A = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|\Psi^+\rangle + |\Psi^-\rangle),
\] \[
|1\rangle_Q|0\rangle_A = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|\Psi^+\rangle - |\Psi^-\rangle), \qquad |1\rangle_Q|1\rangle_A = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|\Phi^+\rangle - |\Phi^-\rangle).
\] Substituting and collecting terms, the full three-qubit state becomes \[
|\Psi_0\rangle = \frac{1}{2}\Bigl[|\Phi^+\rangle_{QA}(\alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle)_B + |\Phi^-\rangle_{QA}(\alpha|0\rangle - \beta|1\rangle)_B
\] \[
\quad + |\Psi^+\rangle_{QA}(\alpha|1\rangle + \beta|0\rangle)_B + |\Psi^-\rangle_{QA}(\alpha|1\rangle - \beta|0\rangle)_B\Bigr].
\]
Step 2: Bell measurement. Alice performs a joint measurement on qubits \(Q\) and \(A\) in the Bell basis, obtaining one of four equally likely outcomes. Each outcome leaves Bob’s qubit in one of four states related to \(|\psi\rangle\) by a known Pauli:



Alice’s outcome
Bob’s state
Correction




\(|\Phi^+\rangle\)
\(\alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle\)
\(\mathbb{I}\)


\(|\Phi^-\rangle\)
\(\alpha|0\rangle - \beta|1\rangle\)

\(\alpha|1\rangle + \beta|0\rangle\)

Step 3: classical communication and correction. Alice sends her two-bit measurement outcome to Bob over a classical channel. Bob applies the corresponding Pauli correction to recover \(|\psi\rangle\) exactly.
Several features deserve emphasis. First, the protocol does not violate no-cloning: Alice’s original state is destroyed by the Bell measurement, so at no point do two copies coexist. Second, it does not allow faster-than-light communication: Bob’s qubit is in the maximally mixed state \(\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{I}\) until he receives Alice’s classical bits, so no information is available to him before the classical message arrives. Third, the protocol consumes the shared entanglement — after teleportation, the Bell pair is gone. Entanglement is thus a fungible resource: one ebit plus two classical bits equals one qubit of quantum communication.

title: Quantum Information and Computation
text:
Quantum Channels

Completely positive trace-preserving maps
A quantum channel is a physically realizable transformation of quantum states. Mathematically, it is a linear map \(\mathcal{E}: \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_A) \to \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_B)\) that is:

Trace-preserving: \(\mathrm{Tr}[\mathcal{E}(\rho)] = \mathrm{Tr}(\rho)\) for all \(\rho\).
Completely positive: \(\mathcal{E} \otimes \mathrm{id}_R\) maps positive operators to positive operators, for any reference system \(R\).

Complete positivity is stronger than positivity and is physically necessary: if Alice applies \(\mathcal{E}\) to her part of an entangled state, the joint state must remain a valid density matrix. The transpose map \(T(\rho) = \rho^T\) is positive but not completely positive — this is the basis of the Peres–Horodecki (PPT) entanglement criterion.


Kraus representation
Theorem (Stinespring, Kraus). A map \(\mathcal{E}\) is a quantum channel if and only if it admits a Kraus decomposition: \[
\mathcal{E}(\rho) = \sum_{k} K_k \rho K_k^\dagger, \qquad \sum_k K_k^\dagger K_k = \mathbb{I}.
\]
The operators \(\{K_k\}\) are called Kraus operators. They are not unique: any set \(\{K_k'\} = \{U_{kl} K_l\}\) related by a unitary matrix gives the same channel.
Physically, the Kraus representation arises from coupling the system to an environment initially in a pure state \(|0\rangle_E\), applying a joint unitary \(U_{SE}\), and tracing out the environment: \[
\mathcal{E}(\rho) = \mathrm{Tr}_E\bigl[U(\rho \otimes |0\rangle\langle 0|)U^\dagger\bigr].
\]
The Kraus operators are \(K_k = \langle k|_E U |0\rangle_E\) for an orthonormal basis \(\{|k\rangle_E\}\).


Example: the depolarizing channel
The depolarizing channel replaces the input state with the maximally mixed state with probability \(p\): \[
\mathcal{E}_p(\rho) = (1-p)\rho + p \cdot \frac{\mathbb{I}}{d}.
\]
For qubits (\(d = 2\)), this can be written in Kraus form using the Pauli matrices: \[
\mathcal{E}_p(\rho) = \left(1 - \frac{3p}{4}\right)\rho + \frac{p}{4}\bigl(\sigma_x \rho \sigma_x + \sigma_y \rho \sigma_y + \sigma_z \rho \sigma_z\bigr).
\]
The depolarizing channel is a useful benchmark: it represents the “worst-case” noise model in the sense that it shrinks the Bloch sphere uniformly. It has quantum capacity zero for \(p \geq 1/2\) (for qubits), reflecting a threshold beyond which no quantum information can be reliably transmitted.

title: Quantum Information and Computation
text:
Quantum Error Correction

The basic idea
Classical information can be protected from noise by redundancy: encode a bit as \(0 \to 000\), \(1 \to 111\), and take a majority vote after transmission. For quantum information, this naive strategy fails — the no-cloning theorem forbids copying an unknown state \(|\psi\rangle\) into \(|\psi\rangle|\psi\rangle|\psi\rangle\). The key insight of quantum error correction (QEC) is that one can instead encode \(k\) logical qubits into \(n\) physical qubits by spreading the quantum information across entangled states, without ever learning or copying the logical state. The resulting \([[n,k,d]]\) code can correct any error affecting up to \(\lfloor(d-1)/2\rfloor\) physical qubits, where \(d\) is the code distance.


The 3-qubit bit-flip code
The simplest quantum code corrects a single bit-flip (\(\sigma_x\)) error. We encode one logical qubit into three physical qubits via \[
|0\rangle_L = |000\rangle, \qquad |1\rangle_L = |111\rangle,
\] so an arbitrary state \(|\psi\rangle = \alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle\) is encoded as \[
|\psi\rangle_L = \alpha|000\rangle + \beta|111\rangle.
\] Note that this is an entangled state of three qubits, not three copies of \(|\psi\rangle\) — no-cloning is respected.
Suppose a bit-flip occurs on the first qubit: \(\alpha|000\rangle + \beta|111\rangle \to \alpha|100\rangle + \beta|011\rangle\). To detect which qubit was flipped without disturbing the encoded information, we measure two syndrome operators: \[
Z_1 Z_2 \quad \text{and} \quad Z_2 Z_3.
\] These operators check whether adjacent pairs of qubits agree, without revealing the values themselves. The syndrome outcomes are:



Error
\(Z_1 Z_2\)
\(Z_2 Z_3\)
Correction




None
\(+1\)
\(+1\)
\(\mathbb{I}\)


\(X_1\)
\(-1\)
\(+1\)
\(\sigma_x^{(1)}\)


\(X_2\)
\(-1\)
\(-1\)
\(\sigma_x^{(2)}\)


\(X_3\)
\(+1\)
\(-1\)
\(\sigma_x^{(3)}\)



The syndrome uniquely identifies the error, and a corrective \(\sigma_x\) on the affected qubit restores the encoded state. Crucially, the syndrome measurement projects onto a subspace without revealing \(\alpha\) or \(\beta\) — it extracts information about the error while preserving the logical state.


The quantum error correction conditions
The 3-qubit code corrects only bit-flip errors. A general \([[n,k,d]]\) code must handle arbitrary errors. The fundamental result is:
Theorem (Knill–Laflamme, 1997). A code with codespace \(\mathcal{C}\) spanned by orthonormal codewords \(\{|\bar{i}\rangle\}\) can correct a set of errors \(\{E_a\}\) if and only if \[
\langle \bar{i}| E_a^\dagger E_b |\bar{j}\rangle = C_{ab}\,\delta_{ij}
\] for some Hermitian matrix \(C_{ab}\) that depends on the errors but not on the codewords \(i, j\).
The \(\delta_{ij}\) condition ensures that errors do not mix different codewords (so that syndrome measurement does not disturb the logical information). The matrix \(C_{ab}\) captures the “overlap” between different errors projected onto the code space; it must be independent of which codeword was encoded.


The Steane code
A practical code must correct both bit-flip (\(\sigma_x\)) and phase-flip (\(\sigma_z\)) errors. The \([[7,1,3]]\) Steane code is the smallest code that does this. It encodes one logical qubit into seven physical qubits and has distance \(d = 3\), so it can correct any single-qubit error (including arbitrary combinations of \(\sigma_x\), \(\sigma_y\), and \(\sigma_z\)). The Steane code is a CSS code (Calderbank–Shor–Steane), meaning it is constructed from two classical codes: one correcting bit-flips and one correcting phase-flips. This modular structure makes CSS codes particularly elegant and amenable to fault-tolerant implementation.


Stabilizer formalism
The most powerful framework for describing quantum codes is the stabilizer formalism (Gottesman, 1997). A stabilizer code is defined by an abelian subgroup \(\mathcal{S}\) of the \(n\)-qubit Pauli group \(\mathcal{P}_n = \{I, X, Y, Z\}^{\otimes n}\) (up to phases) satisfying \(-\mathbb{I} \notin \mathcal{S}\). The codespace is the joint \(+1\) eigenspace of all elements of \(\mathcal{S}\): \[
\mathcal{C} = \{|\psi\rangle \in (\mathbb{C}^2)^{\otimes n} : S|\psi\rangle = +|\psi\rangle \;\; \forall \, S \in \mathcal{S}\}.
\]
If \(\mathcal{S}\) is generated by \(n - k\) independent generators \(g_1, \ldots, g_{n-k}\), the codespace encodes \(k\) logical qubits. Error detection works by measuring the generators: each generator gives a \(\pm 1\) outcome, and the string of outcomes (the syndrome) identifies which error occurred without collapsing the logical state.
For the 3-qubit bit-flip code, the stabilizer group is \(\mathcal{S} = \langle Z_1Z_2,\, Z_2Z_3 \rangle\), with \(n - k = 3 - 1 = 2\) generators — precisely the syndrome operators we encountered above. For the Steane code, \(\mathcal{S}\) has \(7 - 1 = 6\) generators, three detecting \(X\) errors and three detecting \(Z\) errors.


Connection to tensor networks
The stabilizer structure of quantum codes maps naturally to tensor network representations. A stabilizer state (a state stabilized by \(2^n\) independent Pauli operators, i.e., a code with \(k = 0\)) can be represented as a tensor network whose individual tensors encode the stabilizer constraints. More generally, the encoding isometry of a quantum error-correcting code is a tensor that maps \(k\) logical indices to \(n\) physical indices — precisely the structure of a tensor network with one “bulk” layer and one “boundary” layer. This is the foundation of the holographic quantum error-correcting codes discussed in the tensor networks section below, where the bulk-to-boundary map of AdS/CFT is modeled as an isometric tensor network satisfying the quantum error correction conditions.

title: Quantum Information and Computation
text:
Connections to Tensor Networks

MPS as efficiently describable states
A generic state of \(N\) qubits lives in a \(2^N\)-dimensional Hilbert space — exponentially large, and thus intractable to describe classically. However, many physically relevant states (especially ground states of gapped local Hamiltonians in 1D) have limited entanglement and can be efficiently parameterized as matrix product states (MPS): \[
|\psi\rangle = \sum_{i_1, \ldots, i_N} \mathrm{Tr}(A^{i_1} A^{i_2} \cdots A^{i_N}) \, |i_1 i_2 \cdots i_N\rangle,
\] where each \(A^{i_k}\) is a \(\chi \times \chi\) matrix. The parameter \(\chi\), the bond dimension, controls the amount of entanglement the state can carry: the entanglement entropy across any cut is bounded by \(S \leq \log \chi\).
From an information-theoretic standpoint, MPS are the natural class of states that saturate the area law for entanglement entropy in 1D: the entanglement of a contiguous block scales as the size of its boundary (which is a constant in 1D), not the volume of the block.


Area law from information theory
The area law for entanglement entropy is one of the deepest connections between quantum information and many-body physics. For ground states of gapped local Hamiltonians in \(D\) spatial dimensions, one expects \[
S(\rho_A) \sim |\partial A|,
\] where \(|\partial A|\) is the area of the boundary of region \(A\). In 1D, this was rigorously proven by Hastings (2007): gapped ground states satisfy \(S \leq \text{const}\), independent of system size.
The area law explains why tensor network methods work: states with area-law entanglement occupy a tiny corner of the full Hilbert space, and tensor networks are precisely the variational class that parameterizes this corner efficiently.


Quantum error correction and holography
One of the most striking recent developments is the connection between quantum error correction, tensor networks, and holographic duality (AdS/CFT). The Ryu–Takayanagi formula relates the entanglement entropy of a boundary region \(A\) in a holographic CFT to the area of the minimal surface \(\gamma_A\) in the bulk: \[
S(\rho_A) = \frac{\mathrm{Area}(\gamma_A)}{4 G_N}.
\]
This is precisely an area law, and it can be modeled by tensor networks such as the MERA (multiscale entanglement renormalization ansatz) or HaPPY code (Pastawski, Yoshida, Harlow, Preskill, 2015). In the HaPPY model, the bulk-to-boundary map is a quantum error-correcting code: bulk operators in the “entanglement wedge” of a boundary region can be reconstructed from the boundary data, even if part of the boundary is erased.
This perspective suggests that the emergence of spacetime geometry from entanglement is deeply tied to quantum error correction — a beautiful synthesis of quantum information and quantum gravity.
