title: Machine Learning and Neural Networks
text: Machine learning has become an indispensable tool in physics research. But unlike much of the ML literature, which emphasizes benchmarks and engineering, physicists benefit from understanding these methods at the level of mathematical structure — the same way we understand statistical mechanics or quantum field theory. These notes develop the core ideas of modern machine learning with an emphasis on mathematical precision and connections to physics. We start from the foundations of neural networks, work through transformers and attention mechanisms, and then treat generative models (diffusion models and normalizing flows) in detail, drawing on their deep connections to statistical physics. We also cover grokking and manifold learning, two topics where physics intuition provides genuine insight.

title: Machine Learning and Neural Networks
text:
Neural Network Fundamentals

The Universal Approximation Theorem
The theoretical foundation for using neural networks as function approximators rests on the universal approximation theorem. The precise statement (Cybenko, 1989; Hornik, 1991) is:
Theorem. Let \(\sigma: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) be a continuous, non-constant, bounded, monotonically increasing function (e.g., the sigmoid). Let \(I_d = [0, 1]^d\) be the \(d\)-dimensional unit cube, and let \(C(I_d)\) denote the space of continuous functions on \(I_d\) equipped with the supremum norm. Then for any \(f \in C(I_d)\) and any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exist \(N \in \mathbb{N}\), real constants \(w_i, b_i, \alpha_i\) such that the function \[
g(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \alpha_i \, \sigma\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^{d} w_{ij} x_j + b_i\right)
\] satisfies \(\sup_{x \in I_d} |f(x) - g(x)| < \varepsilon\).
In other words, a single hidden layer with sufficiently many neurons can approximate any continuous function on a compact set to arbitrary accuracy. This is an existence theorem: it says nothing about how to find the right weights, nor about how many neurons are needed. The gap between existence and constructive efficiency is where the real difficulty of machine learning lies.
Modern practice uses deep networks (many layers) rather than wide shallow ones, because depth provides exponential efficiency gains for certain function classes. The analogy in physics is the renormalization group: deep networks can implement hierarchical feature extraction, composing simple operations into complex transformations — much as RG coarse-grains short-distance degrees of freedom into effective long-distance descriptions.


Gradient Descent and Backpropagation
Given a parameterized model \(f_\theta(x)\) and a loss function \(\mathcal{L}(\theta)\) measuring the discrepancy between predictions and data, we seek to minimize \(\mathcal{L}\) over parameters \(\theta\). Gradient descent updates: \[
\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \, \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta_t)
\] where \(\eta\) is the learning rate. In practice, we use stochastic gradient descent (SGD), computing gradients on random mini-batches of the data. The stochastic noise in mini-batch gradients turns out to be beneficial — it helps escape shallow local minima and saddle points.
Backpropagation is simply the chain rule applied systematically through the computational graph. For a network with layers \(h_1, h_2, \ldots, h_L\), each computing \(h_\ell = \sigma(W_\ell h_{\ell-1} + b_\ell)\), the gradient of the loss with respect to parameters in layer \(\ell\) involves the product of Jacobians: \[
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W_\ell} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial h_L} \cdot \frac{\partial h_L}{\partial h_{L-1}} \cdots \frac{\partial h_{\ell+1}}{\partial h_\ell} \cdot \frac{\partial h_\ell}{\partial W_\ell}
\]
The computational cost of backpropagation is \(O(1)\) times the cost of a forward pass — this is the key efficiency result that makes training large networks feasible.


Loss Landscapes and Optimization
The loss function \(\mathcal{L}(\theta)\) defines a landscape in the high-dimensional parameter space. Understanding this landscape is essential and connects directly to statistical physics.
In high dimensions, saddle points vastly outnumber local minima. For a random function in \(d\) dimensions, the expected number of saddle points with \(k\) negative eigenvalues grows as \(\binom{d}{k}\), while the number of local minima (\(k = d\)) is exponentially suppressed. This was formalized by Bray and Dean (2007) using random matrix theory and the Kac-Rice formula, connecting directly to the statistical mechanics of disordered systems.
Modern neural networks are typically overparameterized: they have far more parameters than training examples. In this regime, the loss landscape has qualitatively different properties:

Many global minima exist, forming connected low-loss manifolds
Gradient descent finds solutions that generalize well, even without explicit regularization
The implicit bias of SGD favors flat minima (large-volume regions of parameter space), which tend to generalize better

The connection to statistical physics is direct: flat minima correspond to high-entropy regions of parameter space, and SGD acts like a Langevin dynamics at finite temperature, preferentially sampling these regions.


Regularization
To prevent overfitting (memorizing training data noise), several regularization techniques are used:

\(L^2\) regularization (weight decay): Add \(\lambda \|\theta\|^2\) to the loss. This penalizes large weights and acts as a Gaussian prior on parameters in a Bayesian interpretation.
Dropout: Randomly zero out neurons during training. This can be interpreted as training an ensemble of sub-networks and is related to model averaging.
Early stopping: Halt training before the model has fully fit the training data. The number of gradient steps acts as an implicit regularization parameter.
Batch normalization: Normalize layer activations to have zero mean and unit variance. This smooths the loss landscape and stabilizes training.

From a physics perspective, regularization controls the effective complexity of the model, much as a UV cutoff controls the number of degrees of freedom in a field theory.

title: Machine Learning and Neural Networks
text:
Transformers and Attention
The transformer architecture, introduced by Vaswani et al. (2017), has become the dominant architecture in natural language processing and increasingly in scientific applications. Its key innovation is the self-attention mechanism, which allows the model to capture long-range dependencies without the sequential bottleneck of recurrent networks.

The Self-Attention Mechanism
Given an input sequence of \(n\) tokens, each represented by a \(d_{\text{model}}\)-dimensional vector \(x_i\), self-attention computes three sets of vectors through learned linear projections:

Queries: \(Q = XW^Q\), where \(W^Q \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_k}\)
Keys: \(K = XW^K\), where \(W^K \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_k}\)
Values: \(V = XW^V\), where \(W^V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_v}\)

Here \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{\text{model}}}\) is the matrix of input embeddings stacked as rows. The attention output is: \[
\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V
\]
The matrix \(A = \text{softmax}(QK^T / \sqrt{d_k})\) has entries: \[
A_{ij} = \frac{\exp(q_i \cdot k_j / \sqrt{d_k})}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{n} \exp(q_i \cdot k_\ell / \sqrt{d_k})}
\]
Each entry \(A_{ij}\) is a soft attention weight measuring how much token \(i\) attends to token \(j\). The scaling by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) prevents the dot products from becoming large (which would push the softmax into saturation), maintaining stable gradients. This scaling factor is not arbitrary — it ensures the variance of \(q_i \cdot k_j\) is \(O(1)\) when the query and key components are i.i.d. with unit variance.
The physical interpretation is suggestive: the attention matrix \(A\) is a Boltzmann-like distribution. If we write \(E_{ij} = -q_i \cdot k_j\), then \(A_{ij} \propto \exp(-E_{ij}/T)\) with effective temperature \(T = \sqrt{d_k}\). Each token selects what information to gather based on a soft energy minimization.


Multi-Head Attention
Rather than computing a single attention function, multi-head attention runs \(h\) parallel attention heads with different projections: \[
\text{MultiHead}(Q, K, V) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \ldots, \text{head}_h) \, W^O
\] where each head is: \[
\text{head}_i = \text{Attention}(XW_i^Q, XW_i^K, XW_i^V)
\] with separate projection matrices \(W_i^Q \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_k}\), \(W_i^K \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_k}\), \(W_i^V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_v}\) for each head, and an output projection \(W^O \in \mathbb{R}^{hd_v \times d_{\text{model}}}\).
Typically \(d_k = d_v = d_{\text{model}} / h\), so the total computational cost is similar to single-head attention with full dimensionality. Different heads can learn to attend to different aspects of the input — positional relationships, semantic similarity, syntactic structure — in parallel.


Positional Encoding
Since attention is permutation-equivariant (the output is independent of token ordering, up to the reordering itself), positional information must be injected explicitly. Vaswani et al. (2017) used sinusoidal positional encodings: \[
\text{PE}(pos, 2k) = \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2k/d_{\text{model}}}}\right), \qquad \text{PE}(pos, 2k+1) = \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2k/d_{\text{model}}}}\right)
\]
This encoding has a geometric interpretation: each frequency component defines a circle in 2D, and the position is encoded as a point on these circles at different scales. The model can learn to compute relative positions because \(\text{PE}(pos + \Delta)\) is a linear function of \(\text{PE}(pos)\) for any fixed offset \(\Delta\). Modern architectures often use learned positional encodings or relative position representations (e.g., rotary position embeddings), but the sinusoidal encoding illustrates the core idea.


Why Transformers Work for Long-Range Dependencies
Recurrent networks process tokens sequentially: information from token 1 must pass through \(O(n)\) operations to reach token \(n\), leading to vanishing or exploding gradients. Transformers, by contrast, provide \(O(1)\) path length between any pair of tokens through attention. Every token can directly attend to every other token, enabling the model to capture long-range correlations without the information bottleneck of sequential processing.
The computational cost is \(O(n^2 d)\) per layer (due to the \(n \times n\) attention matrix), which limits the sequence length. This is analogous to a mean-field interaction: every spin interacts with every other spin. Various sparse attention patterns (local, strided, learned) reduce this to \(O(n \log n)\) or \(O(n)\), analogous to introducing locality or hierarchy.


Implementation: Self-Attention in PyTorch
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import math

class MultiHeadSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    """Multi-head self-attention mechanism (Vaswani et al., 2017)."""

    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads):
        super().__init__()
        assert d_model % n_heads == 0
        self.d_model = d_model
        self.n_heads = n_heads
        self.d_k = d_model // n_heads

        # Projection matrices for Q, K, V and output
        self.W_q = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)
        self.W_k = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)
        self.W_v = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)
        self.W_o = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)

    def forward(self, x, mask=None):
        """
        Args:
            x: (batch, seq_len, d_model) input embeddings
            mask: optional (batch, seq_len, seq_len) attention mask
        Returns:
            (batch, seq_len, d_model) attention output
        """
        batch_size, seq_len, _ = x.shape

        # Project to queries, keys, values
        Q = self.W_q(x)  # (batch, seq_len, d_model)
        K = self.W_k(x)
        V = self.W_v(x)

        # Reshape for multi-head: (batch, n_heads, seq_len, d_k)
        Q = Q.view(batch_size, seq_len, self.n_heads, self.d_k).transpose(1, 2)
        K = K.view(batch_size, seq_len, self.n_heads, self.d_k).transpose(1, 2)
        V = V.view(batch_size, seq_len, self.n_heads, self.d_k).transpose(1, 2)

        # Scaled dot-product attention
        # scores: (batch, n_heads, seq_len, seq_len)
        scores = torch.matmul(Q, K.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(self.d_k)

        if mask is not None:
            scores = scores.masked_fill(mask == 0, float('-inf'))

        attn_weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)

        # Weighted sum of values
        # output: (batch, n_heads, seq_len, d_k)
        output = torch.matmul(attn_weights, V)

        # Concatenate heads and project
        output = output.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(batch_size, seq_len, self.d_model)
        return self.W_o(output)


# Example usage
d_model, n_heads, seq_len, batch = 64, 8, 20, 4
attn = MultiHeadSelfAttention(d_model, n_heads)
x = torch.randn(batch, seq_len, d_model)
out = attn(x)
print(f"Input shape:  {x.shape}")
print(f"Output shape: {out.shape}")
# Input shape:  torch.Size([4, 20, 64])
# Output shape: torch.Size([4, 20, 64])

title: Machine Learning and Neural Networks
text:
Grokking: Delayed Generalization

The Phenomenon
Power et al. (2022) discovered a surprising phenomenon in neural network training: on small algorithmic datasets (e.g., modular arithmetic, \(a \circ b \pmod{p}\)), networks first memorize the training data perfectly — achieving 100% training accuracy — and then, after many more steps of training, suddenly generalize to the test set. The generalization happens long after the training loss has reached zero, and the transition is sharp: test accuracy jumps from chance level to near-perfect over a narrow window of training steps.
This is grokking: the model memorizes first, then groks (deeply understands) the underlying structure with a dramatic delay.


The Setup
The original experiments used small transformers trained on binary operations in modular arithmetic:

Training data: a fraction (e.g., 50%) of all pairs \((a, b)\) with \(a, b \in \mathbb{Z}_p\)
Task: predict \(a \circ b \pmod{p}\) for operations \(\circ \in \{+, -, \times, /\}\)
The model is trained well past zero training loss with weight decay regularization

The key observation is that without weight decay, the model memorizes and never generalizes. Weight decay is essential — it applies a continuous pressure toward simpler (lower-norm) solutions.


The Mechanistic Interpretability Perspective
Nanda et al. (2023) reverse-engineered what the network learns in the case of modular addition. The network implements a discrete Fourier transform: it learns to represent inputs \(a\) and \(b\) via sinusoidal features \(\cos(2\pi k a/p)\) and \(\sin(2\pi k a/p)\) for various frequencies \(k\). The addition \(a + b \pmod{p}\) is then computed using the trigonometric identity: \[
\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi k(a+b)}{p}\right) = \cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi k a}{p}\right)\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi k b}{p}\right) - \sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi k a}{p}\right)\sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi k b}{p}\right)
\]
The network discovers the Fourier representation through training, even though nothing in the architecture or loss function explicitly encourages it.


Connection to Phase Transitions in Learning
The sharp transition from memorization to generalization is strongly reminiscent of a phase transition. The analogy can be made precise:

Order parameter: Test accuracy (or, more precisely, the mutual information between the learned representation and the true algorithmic structure).
Control parameter: The effective regularization strength, which is a combination of weight decay, training time, and dataset fraction.
Symmetry breaking: The transition from a memorization solution (high-entropy, unstructured) to an algorithmic solution (low-entropy, structured) resembles a symmetry-breaking transition.

Liu et al. (2022) showed that the grokking transition can be understood as a competition between two phases in the loss landscape: a memorization phase with many more solutions (high entropy but high test loss) and a generalization phase with fewer solutions (low entropy but low test loss). Weight decay acts as an effective temperature that tilts the free energy balance. At long training times, the regularization pressure eventually drives the system from the memorization basin to the generalization basin — analogous to a first-order phase transition with a nucleation barrier.
This physics perspective suggests that grokking is not a peculiarity of small algorithmic datasets but a general phenomenon that should occur whenever the generalizing solution is simpler (lower parameter norm) than the memorizing solution.

title: Machine Learning and Neural Networks
text:
Manifold Learning

The Manifold Hypothesis
High-dimensional data — images, molecular configurations, field theory samples — typically lie on or near a low-dimensional manifold embedded in the ambient space. This is the manifold hypothesis. An image of a face in \(\mathbb{R}^{256 \times 256 \times 3}\) is specified by a handful of continuous parameters (pose, lighting, expression, identity), placing it on a manifold of dimension perhaps \(\sim 50\), embedded in a space of dimension \(\sim 200{,}000\).
For physicists, this is familiar: the configuration space of a physical system is constrained by symmetries and conservation laws, and the relevant degrees of freedom are the order parameters — collective coordinates that parameterize the low-dimensional manifold of physically relevant configurations.


Intrinsic Dimension
The intrinsic dimension of a dataset is the dimension of the manifold on which the data concentrates. Estimating it is a nontrivial statistical problem. Common approaches include:

Correlation dimension: Measure how the number of pairs within distance \(r\) scales: \(C(r) \sim r^d\). The exponent \(d\) estimates the intrinsic dimension. This is the same method used to estimate the fractal dimension of strange attractors in dynamical systems.
Maximum likelihood estimation: Levina and Bickel (2004) derived an MLE estimator based on nearest-neighbor distances. For a point \(x_i\) with \(k\)-th nearest neighbor distance \(r_k(x_i)\), the estimator is: \[
\hat{d} = \left[\frac{1}{k-1} \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \log \frac{r_k(x_i)}{r_j(x_i)}\right]^{-1}
\]

In physics, the intrinsic dimension of Monte Carlo samples near a phase transition is related to the number of relevant operators — the critical manifold has a specific dimension determined by the universality class.


PCA as a Baseline
Principal Component Analysis is the simplest dimensionality reduction method. Given data matrix \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) (centered), PCA computes the eigendecomposition of the covariance matrix \(C = X^T X / n\) and projects onto the top \(k\) eigenvectors.
PCA finds the linear subspace that captures maximum variance. It is exact when the data lies on a linear manifold. For nonlinear manifolds, PCA provides a useful baseline: the spectrum of eigenvalues (the scree plot) indicates how many dimensions are needed for a linear approximation, and a gap in the spectrum suggests low intrinsic dimensionality.
In physics, PCA of Monte Carlo configurations can identify the order parameter. For the Ising model, the first principal component of spin configurations near \(T_c\) is highly correlated with the magnetization.


Autoencoders
An autoencoder learns a nonlinear generalization of PCA. It consists of:

An encoder \(f_\theta: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^k\) mapping data to a low-dimensional latent space
A decoder \(g_\phi: \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^d\) mapping back to data space

trained to minimize reconstruction error \(\|x - g_\phi(f_\theta(x))\|^2\). The bottleneck dimension \(k\) forces the network to learn a compressed representation that captures the essential structure.
When applied to physics data (e.g., Ising configurations at various temperatures), the latent variables often discover physically meaningful order parameters without supervision. This connects to the information bottleneck principle: the autoencoder retains the information most relevant for reconstruction while discarding noise.


Visualization: t-SNE and UMAP
For visualizing high-dimensional data in 2D or 3D, two popular methods are:

t-SNE (van der Maaten and Hinton, 2008): Constructs probability distributions over pairs of points in both high-dimensional and low-dimensional spaces, using Gaussian kernels in the original space and Student-t kernels in the embedding. It minimizes the KL divergence between these distributions. t-SNE excels at preserving local structure but can distort global geometry.
UMAP (McInnes et al., 2018): Constructs a fuzzy simplicial set representation of the data and optimizes a low-dimensional embedding that preserves this topological structure. UMAP better preserves global structure than t-SNE and is faster.

Both methods are nonparametric: they produce an embedding of the training points but do not define a mapping for new data. They are visualization tools, not generative models — a distinction that matters when the goal is sampling or density estimation.


Connection to Physics
The manifold hypothesis connects to several ideas in physics:

Configuration space: The physically accessible configurations of a system form a manifold. Constraints (conservation laws, gauge invariance) reduce its dimension.
Order parameters: In Landau theory, the free energy is a function of a few order parameters. These are coordinates on the low-dimensional manifold of macroscopic states.
Slow manifolds: In dynamical systems, the long-time dynamics is confined to a low-dimensional attracting manifold. Learning this manifold from trajectory data is a form of manifold learning.
Latent variables in statistical mechanics: The partition function \(Z = \sum_{\text{micro}} e^{-\beta H}\) can be thought of as integrating out fast modes, leaving only the slow (relevant) variables that parameterize the manifold.

title: Machine Learning and Neural Networks
section: Diffusion Models and Score-Based Generative Modeling
text:
Diffusion Models and Score-Based Generative Modeling
Diffusion models are generative models that learn to reverse a noise-adding process. For physicists, they are Langevin dynamics in disguise — a connection that provides both intuition and computational advantages.

The Physics of Diffusion
Consider a particle undergoing Brownian motion in a potential \(U(x)\). The overdamped Langevin equation is: \[
dx = -\nabla U(x)\, dt + \sqrt{2T}\, dW_t
\]
The particle drifts toward lower potential while being kicked by thermal noise. The stationary distribution is the Boltzmann distribution: \[
p_{\text{eq}}(x) \propto e^{-U(x)/T}
\]


Score Functions and Time Reversal
The score function is defined as: \[
s(x) = \nabla_x \log p(x)
\]
For the Boltzmann distribution, \(s(x) = -\nabla U(x)/T\) — it points in the direction of increasing probability. Anderson (1982) showed that the time-reversed diffusion satisfies: \[
dx = \bigl[s(x, t) + \nabla \cdot D\bigr]\, dt + \sqrt{2T}\, d\bar{W}_t
\] where \(\bar{W}_t\) is a backward Wiener process. If we know the score at each time, we can run the diffusion backward — transforming noise into samples from the data distribution.


The Diffusion Model Recipe
Song et al. (2020) formalized this into a general framework for generative modeling:

Forward process: Gradually add noise to data samples through a stochastic differential equation: \[
x_t = \sqrt{\alpha_t}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \alpha_t}\, \epsilon, \qquad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)
\] where \(\alpha_t\) is a noise schedule decreasing from 1 to 0. At \(t = 0\), we have clean data; at \(t = T\), we have approximately pure Gaussian noise.
Learn the score: Train a neural network \(s_\theta(x_t, t)\) to approximate \(\nabla_x \log p_t(x)\) at each noise level \(t\).
Reverse process: Start from Gaussian noise and iteratively denoise using the learned score.

The training objective (denoising score matching) takes a simple form: \[
\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_0, \epsilon}\!\left[\bigl\|s_\theta(x_t, t) + \epsilon / \sqrt{1 - \alpha_t}\bigr\|^2\right]
\]
The network learns to predict the noise that was added — the score and the noise prediction are related by \(s_\theta(x_t, t) = -\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t) / \sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\).


Physics Applications

Lattice Field Theory
In lattice QCD, we need to sample field configurations from \(p[\phi] \propto e^{-S[\phi]}\), where \(S\) is the lattice action. Standard algorithms like HMC suffer from critical slowing down near the continuum limit and topology freezing (inability to change the topological charge). Diffusion models offer an alternative: learn to directly sample from the target distribution, bypassing Markov chain autocorrelation entirely.
The challenge is that the score function involves the functional derivative \(\delta S / \delta \phi(x)\), and the neural network must respect gauge invariance and other symmetries of the theory.


Spin Systems
For the Ising model \(p(\sigma) \propto \exp(\beta J \sum_{\langle ij \rangle} \sigma_i \sigma_j)\), cluster algorithms are efficient near the critical point. But for frustrated systems (spin glasses, triangular antiferromagnets), where cluster algorithms fail, diffusion models may provide a viable sampling strategy. The approach requires a continuous relaxation of the discrete spin variables.


Molecular Systems
For molecular simulations, diffusion models can generate equilibrium configurations of atomic coordinates directly from the Boltzmann distribution. They can propose collective moves that molecular dynamics misses and learn the free energy landscape. Equivariant architectures respecting SE(3) symmetry are essential for this application.



Implementation: Score Network for 2D Configurations
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class ScoreNetwork(nn.Module):
    """Score network for 2D lattice configurations.

    Uses a ConvNet to respect translation invariance.
    The network predicts the score s(x_t, t) = nabla_x log p_t(x).
    """

    def __init__(self, L, hidden_dim=128, n_layers=4):
        super().__init__()
        self.L = L

        layers = [nn.Conv2d(2, hidden_dim, 3, padding=1), nn.GELU()]
        for _ in range(n_layers - 2):
            layers += [nn.Conv2d(hidden_dim, hidden_dim, 3, padding=1), nn.GELU()]
        layers.append(nn.Conv2d(hidden_dim, 1, 3, padding=1))
        self.net = nn.Sequential(*layers)

    def forward(self, x, t):
        # x: (batch, L, L) configuration
        # t: (batch,) diffusion time
        t_embed = t.view(-1, 1, 1, 1).expand(-1, 1, self.L, self.L)
        inp = torch.cat([x.unsqueeze(1), t_embed], dim=1)
        return self.net(inp).squeeze(1)


def linear_noise_schedule(t, beta_min=0.1, beta_max=20.0):
    """Linear noise schedule: alpha_t = exp(-0.5 * integral of beta(s) ds)."""
    beta_t = beta_min + t * (beta_max - beta_min)
    log_alpha = -0.5 * t * (beta_min + 0.5 * t * (beta_max - beta_min))
    return torch.exp(log_alpha)


def diffusion_loss(model, x0, noise_schedule):
    """Denoising score matching loss."""
    batch_size = x0.shape[0]

    # Sample random diffusion times uniformly
    t = torch.rand(batch_size, device=x0.device)
    alpha_t = noise_schedule(t)

    # Forward process: add noise
    noise = torch.randn_like(x0)
    x_t = torch.sqrt(alpha_t).view(-1, 1, 1) * x0 + \
          torch.sqrt(1 - alpha_t).view(-1, 1, 1) * noise

    # Predict score
    score_pred = model(x_t, t)

    # Target score: -noise / sqrt(1 - alpha_t)
    target = -noise / torch.sqrt(1 - alpha_t).view(-1, 1, 1)

    return ((score_pred - target) ** 2).mean()


@torch.no_grad()
def sample_langevin(model, noise_schedule, L, n_steps=500, batch_size=16, device='cpu'):
    """Generate samples by running the reverse diffusion (Langevin dynamics)."""
    x = torch.randn(batch_size, L, L, device=device)
    dt = 1.0 / n_steps

    for i in reversed(range(n_steps)):
        t = torch.full((batch_size,), (i + 0.5) * dt, device=device)
        score = model(x, t)

        # Reverse SDE Euler-Maruyama step
        noise = torch.randn_like(x) if i > 0 else torch.zeros_like(x)
        x = x + (score) * dt + torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(2.0 * dt)) * noise

    return x

title: Machine Learning and Neural Networks
text:
Normalizing Flows
While diffusion models learn the score function and generate samples iteratively, normalizing flows learn an explicit invertible map \(f: \mathcal{Z} \to \mathcal{X}\) from a simple base distribution (e.g., Gaussian) to the target distribution. The density is given exactly by the change of variables formula: \[
p_X(x) = p_Z\!\left(f^{-1}(x)\right) \left|\det \frac{\partial f^{-1}}{\partial x}\right|
\]
This is the same change-of-variables formula from classical mechanics and thermodynamics — the Jacobian determinant accounts for the volume distortion of the map.

Advantages for Physics
Normalizing flows have specific advantages for physics applications:

Exact density evaluation: The log-probability \(\log p_X(x)\) can be computed exactly, enabling importance sampling and reweighting. This is crucial for computing expectation values \(\langle O \rangle = \int O(x) p(x) dx\) using samples from the flow.
Explicit samples: No iterative denoising is needed; a single forward pass through \(f\) generates a sample.
Tractable KL divergence: The flow can be trained by minimizing the KL divergence to the target distribution \(\pi(x) \propto e^{-S(x)}\) directly, without requiring training data: \[
D_{\text{KL}}(p_X \| \pi) = \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_Z}\!\left[\log p_X(f(z)) - \log \pi(f(z))\right]
\]

This self-training approach is particularly powerful for physics, where we know the target distribution (the Boltzmann weight) but cannot easily sample from it.


RealNVP Architecture
RealNVP (Real-valued Non-Volume Preserving transformations; Dinh et al., 2017) is a widely used flow architecture, especially for lattice field theory. Each coupling layer splits the input \(x\) into two groups using a binary mask \(b\):
\[
y_A = x_A, \qquad y_B = x_B \odot \exp\!\left(s(x_A)\right) + t(x_A)
\]
where \(x_A = b \odot x\) and \(x_B = (1-b) \odot x\) are the masked and unmasked components, and \(s\) and \(t\) are arbitrary neural networks (scale and translation). The Jacobian is triangular, so its determinant is simply: \[
\log \left|\det \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\right| = \sum_{i \in B} s_i(x_A)
\]
This is \(O(d)\) to compute, avoiding the \(O(d^3)\) cost of a general Jacobian determinant.
class AffineCouplingLayer(nn.Module):
    """Affine coupling layer (RealNVP) for lattice field configurations."""

    def __init__(self, mask, hidden_dim=64):
        super().__init__()
        self.register_buffer('mask', mask)

        self.s_net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(1, hidden_dim, 3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Conv2d(hidden_dim, hidden_dim, 3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Conv2d(hidden_dim, 1, 3, padding=1),
            nn.Tanh(),  # Bounded scale for stability
        )
        self.t_net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(1, hidden_dim, 3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Conv2d(hidden_dim, hidden_dim, 3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Conv2d(hidden_dim, 1, 3, padding=1),
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        """Forward pass: z -> x direction."""
        x_masked = x * self.mask
        s = self.s_net(x_masked.unsqueeze(1)).squeeze(1)
        t = self.t_net(x_masked.unsqueeze(1)).squeeze(1)

        y = x_masked + (1 - self.mask) * (x * torch.exp(s) + t)
        log_det = ((1 - self.mask) * s).sum(dim=(1, 2))

        return y, log_det

    def inverse(self, y):
        """Inverse pass: x -> z direction."""
        y_masked = y * self.mask
        s = self.s_net(y_masked.unsqueeze(1)).squeeze(1)
        t = self.t_net(y_masked.unsqueeze(1)).squeeze(1)

        x = y_masked + (1 - self.mask) * (y - t) * torch.exp(-s)
        log_det = -((1 - self.mask) * s).sum(dim=(1, 2))

        return x, log_det


class NormalizingFlow(nn.Module):
    """Stack of coupling layers with alternating masks."""

    def __init__(self, L, n_layers=8, hidden_dim=64):
        super().__init__()
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList()
        for i in range(n_layers):
            # Checkerboard mask, alternating between layers
            mask = self._checkerboard_mask(L, parity=i % 2)
            self.layers.append(AffineCouplingLayer(mask, hidden_dim))

    def _checkerboard_mask(self, L, parity=0):
        mask = torch.zeros(L, L)
        mask[::2, ::2] = 1
        mask[1::2, 1::2] = 1
        if parity:
            mask = 1 - mask
        return mask

    def forward(self, z):
        """Map from base distribution to target."""
        log_det_total = 0
        x = z
        for layer in self.layers:
            x, log_det = layer(x)
            log_det_total += log_det
        return x, log_det_total


Flows for Lattice Field Theory
Albergo et al. (2019) demonstrated that normalizing flows can generate independent samples for lattice \(\phi^4\) theory, completely eliminating autocorrelation. The approach trains a flow to map a Gaussian base distribution to the Boltzmann distribution \(p[\phi] \propto e^{-S[\phi]}\), using the known action \(S[\phi]\) to compute the KL divergence loss without needing pre-generated training data.
Noe et al. (2019) introduced Boltzmann generators, applying normalizing flows to sample equilibrium configurations of molecular systems. By training on short MD trajectories and the known energy function, the flow learns to generate diverse configurations that bridge between metastable states — a task that would require prohibitively long MD simulations.
The key challenge for flows in physics is the invertibility constraint, which limits architectural expressiveness. Continuous normalizing flows (neural ODEs) relax this constraint somewhat but introduce other computational costs.

title: Machine Learning and Neural Networks
text:
Physics-ML Connections
The connections between machine learning and statistical physics run deeper than analogy. Several precise mappings exist.

Loss Landscapes as Energy Landscapes
The loss function \(\mathcal{L}(\theta)\) defines an energy landscape over parameter space. The training dynamics seek low-loss configurations, just as physical systems relax to low-energy states. The correspondence is:



Machine Learning
Statistical Physics




Parameters \(\theta\)
Microscopic configuration


Loss \(\mathcal{L}(\theta)\)
Energy \(E(\mathcal{C})\)


Learning rate \(\eta\)
Inverse temperature \(\beta\)


Mini-batch noise
Thermal fluctuations


Flat minima
High-entropy states


Sharp minima
Low-entropy states



This correspondence is not merely metaphorical. The PAC-Bayesian generalization bound states that the generalization gap is controlled by the KL divergence between the learned distribution and a prior — which, in the statistical mechanics formulation, is the free energy difference. Flat minima occupy more volume in parameter space (higher entropy), leading to lower free energy and better generalization.


SGD as Langevin Dynamics
Stochastic gradient descent with mini-batch noise obeys: \[
\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta_t) + \sqrt{\eta}\, \xi_t
\] where \(\xi_t\) is the noise from mini-batch sampling. In the continuous-time limit, this is an overdamped Langevin equation: \[
d\theta = -\nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta)\, dt + \sqrt{2T_{\text{eff}}}\, dW_t
\] with an effective temperature \(T_{\text{eff}} \propto \eta \cdot \text{(gradient noise covariance)}\). The learning rate controls the temperature: large learning rates explore more of the landscape (high temperature), while learning rate annealing corresponds to simulated annealing.
This connection has been made rigorous by Mandt et al. (2017), who showed that SGD with constant learning rate converges to a stationary distribution that approximates a Gibbs distribution \(p(\theta) \propto \exp(-\mathcal{L}(\theta)/T_{\text{eff}})\).


Phase Transitions in Learning
Learning dynamics exhibit phase transitions as hyperparameters or dataset properties change:

Double descent: Test error first decreases (classical bias-variance trade-off), then increases at the interpolation threshold (where the model just fits the training data), then decreases again as the model becomes increasingly overparameterized. This non-monotonic behavior resembles a phase transition at the interpolation threshold, where the system changes from underfitting to overfitting to implicit regularization regimes.
Feature learning transitions: As network width, depth, or training time increases, there can be sharp transitions where the network discovers structure in the data. The grokking phenomenon discussed above is one example. Another is the transition from lazy (kernel) regime to rich (feature-learning) regime as network width varies.
Scaling laws: The loss of large language models scales as a power law in model size, dataset size, and compute: \(\mathcal{L} \sim N^{-\alpha}\). Power-law scaling is characteristic of systems near criticality, and recent work has explored whether neural scaling laws can be understood through the lens of critical phenomena and renormalization group theory.



Information Geometry
The parameter space of a statistical model carries a natural Riemannian metric, the Fisher information metric: \[
g_{ij} = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\partial \log p(x|\theta)}{\partial \theta_i} \frac{\partial \log p(x|\theta)}{\partial \theta_j}\right]
\]
Natural gradient descent uses this metric to move in the steepest direction in distribution space (not parameter space): \[
\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \, g^{-1}(\theta_t) \nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta_t)
\]
The Fisher metric is the unique metric (up to scaling) that is invariant under reparameterization. In physics terms, it is the metric on the space of probability distributions induced by the KL divergence, just as the metric on configuration space is induced by the action. This geometric perspective connects optimization in ML to the geometry of thermodynamic state spaces.

title: Machine Learning and Neural Networks
text:
Summary and Outlook
The ideas in these notes share a common thread: machine learning methods become most transparent and most powerful when understood through the lens of physics. Diffusion models are Langevin dynamics. SGD is a thermal process exploring an energy landscape. Grokking is a phase transition. The manifold hypothesis is a statement about the effective dimensionality of configuration space.
For a physicist learning ML, the recommendation is: do not treat these methods as black boxes. The mathematical structures — stochastic processes, statistical mechanics, differential geometry, information theory — are the same ones that appear throughout physics. Understanding them deeply, as these notes attempt to do, is the path to both using ML methods effectively and contributing new ideas to the field.

title: Mirror Symmetry and T-Duality
text:
Mirror symmetry is one of the most profound and surprising discoveries to emerge from string theory. At its core, it asserts that two topologically distinct Calabi–Yau manifolds can give rise to identical physics when used as string compactification backgrounds. What began as a computational coincidence in the late 1980s has since grown into a deep mathematical subject, connecting enumerative geometry, symplectic topology, algebraic geometry, and homological algebra.
These notes give an overview of the key ideas: T-duality as the simplest string duality, mirror symmetry as a generalization thereof, the SYZ conjecture that connects the two, and the role of D-branes. We work at a level of detail appropriate for someone who has seen the basics of string theory and wants to understand how mirror symmetry fits together.

title: Mirror Symmetry and T-Duality
text:
T-Duality: The Simplest String Duality

Circle compactification
Consider a closed bosonic string propagating on a spacetime where one direction is compactified on a circle of radius \(R\). The center-of-mass momentum along the circle is quantized: \[
p = \frac{n}{R}, \qquad n \in \mathbb{Z},
\] since the wavefunction must be single-valued, \(e^{ipX} = e^{ip(X+2\pi R)}\). But strings, unlike point particles, can also wind around the circle. The winding contribution to the energy depends on the string length stretched around the circle: \[
E_{\text{winding}} \propto \frac{w R}{\alpha'}, \qquad w \in \mathbb{Z},
\] where \(w\) is the winding number and \(\alpha' = l_s^2\) is the Regge slope.
The full mass formula for a string on \(\mathbb{R}^{1,d-1} \times S^1\) is \[
m^2 = \frac{n^2}{R^2} + \frac{w^2 R^2}{\alpha'^2} + \frac{2}{\alpha'}(N_L + N_R - 2),
\] with the level-matching condition \(N_L - N_R = nw\).


The duality
The spectrum is invariant under the simultaneous exchange \[
R \;\longleftrightarrow\; \frac{\alpha'}{R}, \qquad n \;\longleftrightarrow\; w.
\]
This is T-duality. A string propagating on a circle of radius \(R\) sees exactly the same physics as a string on a circle of radius \(\alpha'/R\), provided we exchange momentum modes with winding modes. In particular, the self-dual radius \(R = \sqrt{\alpha'}\) is a special point where the theory has enhanced \(SU(2)_L \times SU(2)_R\) gauge symmetry.
T-duality is not merely a classical statement: it is an exact equivalence of the full quantum string theory, order by order in the string coupling \(g_s\). It relates large and small geometries, demonstrating that string theory has a minimum meaningful length scale \(\sim \sqrt{\alpha'}\).


Detailed example: free boson on a circle
To see T-duality concretely, consider the worldsheet action for a single free boson \(X\) compactified on a circle of radius \(R\), so that \(X \sim X + 2\pi R\). The mode expansion on a closed string worldsheet (with worldsheet coordinates \(\sigma \in [0, 2\pi)\) and Euclidean time \(\tau\)) is \[
X(\tau, \sigma) = x_0 + \frac{\alpha' p}{2}\tau + w R \sigma + \frac{i}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\alpha'}{2}} \sum_{n \neq 0} \left( \frac{\alpha_n}{n} e^{-in(\tau + \sigma)} + \frac{\tilde{\alpha}_n}{n} e^{-in(\tau - \sigma)} \right),
\] where \(x_0\) is the center-of-mass position, \(p = n/R\) is the quantized momentum (\(n \in \mathbb{Z}\)), \(w \in \mathbb{Z}\) is the winding number, and \(\alpha_n\), \(\tilde{\alpha}_n\) are the left- and right-moving oscillator modes satisfying \([\alpha_m, \alpha_n] = m\,\delta_{m+n,0}\) and similarly for \(\tilde{\alpha}_n\).
It is illuminating to decompose \(X\) into left- and right-moving parts, \(X = X_L(\tau + \sigma) + X_R(\tau - \sigma)\), with \[
X_L = \frac{x_0}{2} + \frac{\alpha'}{2} p_L (\tau + \sigma) + \text{oscillators}, \qquad X_R = \frac{x_0}{2} + \frac{\alpha'}{2} p_R (\tau - \sigma) + \text{oscillators},
\] where the left- and right-moving momenta are \[
p_L = \frac{n}{R} + \frac{wR}{\alpha'}, \qquad p_R = \frac{n}{R} - \frac{wR}{\alpha'}.
\] The mass-shell condition for the closed string then gives the spacetime mass \[
m^2 = p_L^2 + p_R^2 + \frac{2}{\alpha'}(N_L + N_R - 2) = \frac{n^2}{R^2} + \frac{w^2 R^2}{\alpha'^2} + \frac{2}{\alpha'}(N_L + N_R - 2),
\] together with the level-matching constraint \(N_L - N_R = nw\), which follows from the requirement that \(p_L^2 - p_R^2 = 4nw/\alpha'\) be compensated by the oscillator contributions.
The key observation is that the spectrum depends on \(n\) and \(w\) only through the combination \(n^2/R^2 + w^2 R^2/\alpha'^2\), which is manifestly invariant under the simultaneous exchange \[
R \to \frac{\alpha'}{R}, \qquad n \leftrightarrow w.
\] At the level of the left- and right-moving momenta, this acts as \(p_L \to p_L\), \(p_R \to -p_R\), or equivalently \(X_R \to -X_R\) while leaving \(X_L\) unchanged. This asymmetric action on the worldsheet is the hallmark of T-duality: it is a parity transformation on the right-movers only.
The partition function on the torus (the one-loop vacuum amplitude) can be written as a sum over the Narain lattice \(\Gamma_{1,1}\) of left- and right-moving momenta \((p_L, p_R)\), and T-duality is an \(O(1,1;\mathbb{Z})\) automorphism of this lattice. For compactification on \(T^d\), this generalizes to \(O(d,d;\mathbb{Z})\), the T-duality group acting on the Narain lattice \(\Gamma_{d,d}\).


T-duality and type II strings
For superstrings, T-duality has an additional twist: it exchanges the two type II theories.

Type IIA on \(S^1\) of radius \(R\) \(\;\longleftrightarrow\;\) Type IIB on \(S^1\) of radius \(\alpha'/R\).

The reason is that T-duality acts on the right-moving worldsheet fermions by a sign flip, which exchanges the GSO projections of IIA and IIB. This already hints at mirror symmetry: if T-duality along one circle exchanges IIA and IIB, what happens when we T-dualize along three circles simultaneously?

title: Mirror Symmetry and T-Duality
text:
Calabi–Yau Geometry Primer
Before discussing mirror symmetry, we collect the essential geometric background on Calabi–Yau manifolds.

Definition and equivalent characterizations
A Calabi–Yau manifold of complex dimension \(n\) is a compact Kahler manifold \((X, g, J, \omega)\) satisfying any of the following equivalent conditions (by Yau’s theorem, proving the Calabi conjecture):

Vanishing first Chern class: \(c_1(X) = 0\) in \(H^2(X, \mathbb{R})\).
Ricci-flat Kahler metric: there exists a Kahler metric with \(\mathrm{Ric}(g) = 0\).
\(SU(n)\) holonomy: the holonomy group of \(g\) is contained in \(SU(n)\).
Trivial canonical bundle: \(K_X = \Lambda^n T^*X \cong \mathcal{O}_X\), i.e., there exists a nowhere-vanishing holomorphic \(n\)-form \(\Omega\).

The existence of the Ricci-flat metric is guaranteed by Yau’s theorem (1978): given any Kahler class \([\omega]\) on a compact Kahler manifold with \(c_1 = 0\), there exists a unique Ricci-flat Kahler metric in that class. This metric is not known explicitly in any non-trivial compact example, but its existence is sufficient for many applications.
For string theory, we primarily care about Calabi–Yau threefolds (\(n = 3\)), which provide the six extra dimensions needed to compactify ten-dimensional superstring theory to four dimensions while preserving \(\mathcal{N} = 2\) supersymmetry.


The Hodge diamond
On a compact Kahler manifold of complex dimension \(n\), the Dolbeault cohomology groups \(H^{p,q}(X)\) have dimensions \(h^{p,q} = \dim H^{p,q}(X)\), arranged in the Hodge diamond. For a Calabi–Yau threefold, the existence of \(\Omega\) and the Kahler condition impose strong constraints. The Hodge diamond simplifies to: \[
\begin{array}{ccccccc}
& & & 1 & & & \\
& & 0 & & 0 & & \\
& 0 & & h^{1,1} & & 0 & \\
1 & & h^{2,1} & & h^{2,1} & & 1 \\
& 0 & & h^{1,1} & & 0 & \\
& & 0 & & 0 & & \\
& & & 1 & & & \\
\end{array}
\] Here we have used: \(h^{0,0} = h^{3,3} = 1\) (connectedness), \(h^{1,0} = h^{0,1} = 0\) (for strict \(SU(3)\) holonomy), \(h^{3,0} = h^{0,3} = 1\) (from \(\Omega\)), \(h^{2,0} = h^{0,2} = 0\), and Serre duality \(h^{p,q} = h^{n-p, n-q}\). The only independent Hodge numbers are \(h^{1,1}\) and \(h^{2,1}\).


Moduli: Kahler and complex structure
The two independent Hodge numbers have direct geometric and physical interpretations:
Kahler moduli (\(h^{1,1}\)): The Kahler form \(\omega\) is a closed real \((1,1)\)-form, and \(H^{1,1}(X, \mathbb{R})\) parametrizes the deformations of \(\omega\) within the Kahler cone. Choosing a basis \(\{e_i\}\) of \(H^{1,1}(X, \mathbb{Z})\), we write \(\omega = \sum_{i=1}^{h^{1,1}} t^i e_i\) where \(t^i > 0\) are the Kahler parameters. Physically, these control the volumes of holomorphic 2-cycles (and hence 4-cycles by Poincare duality). In string theory, these are complexified by the \(B\)-field: \(t^i_{\mathbb{C}} = \int_{C_i} (B + i\omega)\).
Complex structure moduli (\(h^{2,1}\)): By the Kodaira–Spencer theory, infinitesimal deformations of the complex structure of \(X\) are classified by \(H^1(X, TX) \cong H^{2,1}(X)\) (using the contraction with \(\Omega\) to identify \(TX \cong \Omega^2_X\)). There are \(h^{2,1}\) independent ways to deform the shape of \(X\) while preserving the Calabi–Yau condition. These deformations change the periods \(\int_{\gamma} \Omega\) of the holomorphic 3-form over 3-cycles \(\gamma \in H_3(X, \mathbb{Z})\).
The total number of massless scalar fields in the four-dimensional \(\mathcal{N} = 2\) theory is \(h^{1,1} + h^{2,1}\) (plus the dilaton and the dual of the \(B\)-field), organized into \(h^{1,1}\) vector multiplets and \(h^{2,1}\) hypermultiplets (or vice versa, depending on whether we compactify type IIA or type IIB).

title: Mirror Symmetry and T-Duality
text:
Mirror Symmetry

Calabi–Yau compactification
To obtain \(\mathcal{N} = 2\) supersymmetry in four dimensions from type II strings in ten dimensions, we compactify on a Calabi–Yau threefold \(X\) — a compact Kahler manifold of complex dimension 3 with vanishing first Chern class (equivalently, with \(SU(3)\) holonomy). The topology of \(X\) determines the low-energy spectrum, and the relevant topological data is captured by the Hodge numbers \(h^{p,q}(X)\).
For a Calabi–Yau threefold, the independent Hodge numbers reduce to two: \(h^{1,1}\) and \(h^{2,1}\). These count, respectively:

\(h^{1,1}\): the number of Kahler moduli (deformations of the size and shape of 2-cycles),
\(h^{2,1}\): the number of complex structure moduli (deformations of the shape of 3-cycles).

The Euler characteristic is \(\chi = 2(h^{1,1} - h^{2,1})\).


The mirror phenomenon
Mirror symmetry asserts that for every Calabi–Yau threefold \(X\), there exists a mirror Calabi–Yau \(\widetilde{X}\) such that \[
h^{1,1}(X) = h^{2,1}(\widetilde{X}), \qquad h^{2,1}(X) = h^{1,1}(\widetilde{X}).
\]
The Hodge diamond is reflected, hence the name. Since the Euler characteristics satisfy \(\chi(\widetilde{X}) = -\chi(X)\), the mirror partners are topologically distinct.
The physical content is deeper than a numerical coincidence: the full string theories are equivalent, \[
\text{Type IIA on } X \quad \longleftrightarrow \quad \text{Type IIB on } \widetilde{X}.
\]
Under this duality, the Kahler moduli space of \(X\) is identified with the complex structure moduli space of \(\widetilde{X}\), and vice versa. Quantities that are difficult to compute on one side (because they receive quantum corrections) become classical computations on the mirror side.


Why mirror symmetry matters: enumerative geometry
The most celebrated early application was the computation of the number of rational curves on the quintic threefold. Consider the quintic \(X \subset \mathbb{CP}^4\), defined as the zero locus of a degree-5 polynomial. It has \(h^{1,1} = 1\) and \(h^{2,1} = 101\).
Candelas, de la Ossa, Green, and Parkes (1991) used mirror symmetry to compute the genus-zero prepotential on the Kahler moduli space of \(X\), which encodes the numbers \(n_d\) of rational curves of degree \(d\): \[
\mathcal{F} = \frac{5}{6}t^3 + \sum_{d=1}^{\infty} n_d \, \mathrm{Li}_3(e^{-dt}),
\] where \(t\) is the complexified Kahler parameter and \(\mathrm{Li}_3\) is the trilogarithm. On the mirror side, \(\widetilde{X}\) has \(h^{1,1} = 101\) and \(h^{2,1} = 1\), and the prepotential is determined by the periods of the holomorphic 3-form \(\Omega\) — a classical computation involving Picard–Fuchs differential equations.
The result: \(n_1 = 2875\), \(n_2 = 609250\), \(n_3 = 317206375\), and so on. The degree-3 number had been recently computed by algebraic geometers (Ellingsrud and Stromme) and initially disagreed with the physics prediction. After a bug in the mathematicians’ code was found and fixed, the numbers agreed. This was a dramatic early confirmation of mirror symmetry.

title: Mirror Symmetry and T-Duality
text:
The SYZ Conjecture

Statement
Strominger, Yau, and Zaslow (1996) proposed a geometric explanation for mirror symmetry:
SYZ Conjecture. A Calabi–Yau threefold \(X\) admitting a mirror partner \(\widetilde{X}\) has a special Lagrangian \(T^3\) fibration \[
T^3 \hookrightarrow X \xrightarrow{\pi} B,
\] where \(B\) is a 3-dimensional base. The mirror \(\widetilde{X}\) is obtained by T-dualizing the \(T^3\) fibers.
A special Lagrangian submanifold \(L\) of a Calabi–Yau \(X\) is a real 3-dimensional submanifold satisfying two conditions:

\(\omega|_L = 0\) (Lagrangian condition, where \(\omega\) is the Kahler form),
\(\mathrm{Im}(e^{i\theta}\Omega)|_L = 0\) for some phase \(\theta\) (special condition, where \(\Omega\) is the holomorphic 3-form).



Physical reasoning
The SYZ conjecture generalizes T-duality from a single circle to three circles simultaneously. On a torus \(T^3\) of radii \(R_1, R_2, R_3\), performing T-duality on all three circles gives a dual torus with radii \(\alpha'/R_1, \alpha'/R_2, \alpha'/R_3\). Since T-duality along a single circle exchanges type IIA and IIB, T-duality along three circles (an odd number) again exchanges IIA and IIB — exactly what mirror symmetry does.
The SYZ picture is most reliable in the large complex structure limit of \(X\) (equivalently the large volume limit of \(\widetilde{X}\)), where the \(T^3\) fibers are large and the T-duality along each circle is well-defined. Away from this limit, quantum corrections modify the picture, and singular fibers (where the torus degenerates) play an important role.


Singular fibers and quantum corrections
In practice, the SYZ fibration always has singular fibers over a codimension-2 locus \(\Delta \subset B\) (the discriminant locus). Near these singular fibers, the semiclassical T-duality picture breaks down, and one must account for contributions from holomorphic discs with boundary on the Lagrangian fibers. These disc instanton corrections are responsible for much of the richness of mirror symmetry.
The discriminant locus \(\Delta\) is generically a trivalent graph (in the case of a threefold), and the singular fibers above \(\Delta\) are tori with collapsed cycles. The simplest degeneration is the Kodaira type \(I_1\) fiber, where a single 1-cycle of \(T^3\) pinches to zero size, producing a nodal torus. More complicated singularities occur at the vertices of the graph \(\Delta\), where multiple cycles degenerate simultaneously.
The physical importance of singular fibers is as follows. A D-brane (say a D2-brane in type IIA) wrapping a holomorphic disc \(D\) with boundary \(\partial D\) on a Lagrangian fiber \(L_b\) contributes a factor \(\exp(-\int_D \omega)\) to the effective action. These disc instantons correct the naive T-duality transformation in a crucial way: without them, the dual torus fibers would glue together incorrectly, and the mirror \(\widetilde{X}\) would not be a Kahler manifold.
More precisely, consider the complexified symplectic area \(A = \int_D (B + i\omega)\) of a holomorphic disc. The generating function of disc instanton contributions defines a superpotential on the moduli space of the Lagrangian fiber: \[
W(L_b) = \sum_{\beta \in \pi_2(X, L_b)} n_\beta \, e^{-A(\beta)},
\] where \(n_\beta\) is an open Gromov–Witten invariant counting discs in the class \(\beta\). These corrections are localized near the discriminant locus: far from \(\Delta\), the fibers are smooth and have no holomorphic discs ending on them (by a monotonicity argument), so the naive T-duality is valid. The non-trivial corrections arise only as one approaches the singular fibers.
The program of making the SYZ construction rigorous, incorporating these quantum corrections, has been carried out in detail for toric Calabi–Yau manifolds (by Gross and Siebert using tropical geometry, and by Auroux using symplectic techniques) and remains an active area of research for compact Calabi–Yaus. The key insight from this program is that the quantum-corrected SYZ mirror is constructed not by naive fiberwise T-duality, but by a wall-crossing procedure: as one crosses walls of marginal stability (real codimension-1 loci in \(B\) emanating from \(\Delta\)), the gluing of the dual torus fibers jumps by symplectomorphisms determined by the disc counts.

title: Mirror Symmetry and T-Duality
text:
The Quintic and Its Mirror

The quintic threefold
The quintic threefold is the hypersurface \[
X_5 = \left\{ [z_0 : z_1 : z_2 : z_3 : z_4] \in \mathbb{CP}^4 \;\middle|\; z_0^5 + z_1^5 + z_2^5 + z_3^5 + z_4^5 + \text{lower-order terms} = 0 \right\},
\] defined as the zero locus of a generic homogeneous polynomial of degree 5 in the five homogeneous coordinates of \(\mathbb{CP}^4\). By the Lefschetz hyperplane theorem and adjunction, \(X_5\) is a smooth Calabi–Yau threefold: the canonical bundle is \(K_{X_5} = \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{CP}^4}(-5)|_{X_5} \otimes \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{CP}^4}(5)|_{X_5} = \mathcal{O}_{X_5}\), confirming \(c_1 = 0\).
The Hodge numbers are computed from the Lefschetz theorem and residue calculus: \[
h^{1,1}(X_5) = 1, \qquad h^{2,1}(X_5) = 101.
\] The single Kahler modulus corresponds to the overall size of the quintic (inherited from the hyperplane class of \(\mathbb{CP}^4\)). The 101 complex structure moduli parametrize the choice of degree-5 polynomial: the space of such polynomials has dimension \(\binom{5+4}{4} = 126\), modulo the \(\dim PGL(5) = 24\) coordinate reparametrizations, giving \(126 - 24 - 1 = 101\) independent deformations (the \(-1\) accounts for overall rescaling). The Euler characteristic is \(\chi = 2(1 - 101) = -200\).


The Greene–Plesser mirror construction
The mirror of the quintic was constructed by Greene and Plesser (1990) using an orbifold procedure. Consider the special one-parameter subfamily (the Fermat pencil) \[
X_\psi: \quad z_0^5 + z_1^5 + z_2^5 + z_3^5 + z_4^5 - 5\psi \, z_0 z_1 z_2 z_3 z_4 = 0,
\] and define the group \(G = (\mathbb{Z}_5)^3\), realized as the subgroup of \((\mathbb{Z}_5)^4\) acting by \[
(z_0, z_1, z_2, z_3, z_4) \mapsto (\omega^{a_1} z_0, \omega^{a_2} z_1, \omega^{a_3} z_2, \omega^{a_4} z_3, z_4), \qquad \omega = e^{2\pi i/5},
\] where \((a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4) \in (\mathbb{Z}_5)^4\) with \(a_1 + a_2 + a_3 + a_4 \equiv 0 \pmod{5}\) (this condition ensures the polynomial \(X_\psi\) is invariant), modulo the overall diagonal action \((1,1,1,1,1)\) which acts trivially on \(\mathbb{CP}^4\). The mirror quintic is obtained as the crepant resolution of the quotient: \[
\widetilde{X}_5 = \widehat{X_\psi / G}.
\] The orbifold action collapses most of the complex structure moduli but introduces new Kahler moduli from the resolution of singularities. The result has Hodge numbers \[
h^{1,1}(\widetilde{X}_5) = 101, \qquad h^{2,1}(\widetilde{X}_5) = 1,
\] confirming the mirror exchange \(h^{1,1} \leftrightarrow h^{2,1}\).


Periods and the Picard–Fuchs equation
The single complex structure parameter \(\psi\) of \(\widetilde{X}_5\) maps to the complexified Kahler parameter of \(X_5\). The holomorphic 3-form \(\Omega(\psi)\) on \(\widetilde{X}_5\) has periods \(\Pi_i(\psi) = \int_{\gamma_i} \Omega\) over a symplectic basis \(\{\gamma_i\}\) of \(H_3(\widetilde{X}_5, \mathbb{Z})\). These periods satisfy a fourth-order Picard–Fuchs differential equation in the variable \(z = (5\psi)^{-5}\): \[
\left[ \theta^4 - 5z(5\theta + 1)(5\theta + 2)(5\theta + 3)(5\theta + 4) \right] \Pi(z) = 0, \qquad \theta = z\frac{d}{dz}.
\] Near the large complex structure point \(z = 0\) (equivalently \(\psi \to \infty\)), the four independent solutions have the structure \(\Pi_0 = 1 + \mathcal{O}(z)\), \(\Pi_1 = \Pi_0 \log z + \mathcal{O}(z)\), and two further solutions involving \((\log z)^2\) and \((\log z)^3\). The mirror map \(t(z) = \Pi_1/\Pi_0\) identifies the flat coordinate \(t\) on the Kahler moduli space of \(X_5\), and the prepotential \(\mathcal{F}(t)\) is extracted from the ratios of periods.

title: Mirror Symmetry and T-Duality
text:
Mirror Symmetry and Enumerative Geometry
The deepest computational power of mirror symmetry lies in the relationship between the A-model on \(X\) and the B-model on \(\widetilde{X}\). These are two topologically twisted versions of the \(\mathcal{N} = (2,2)\) worldsheet sigma model, each capturing different geometric information.

The A-model: Gromov–Witten invariants
The A-model on a Calabi–Yau \(X\) depends only on the Kahler (symplectic) structure of \(X\), and its observables are the Gromov–Witten invariants. At genus zero, the relevant objects are holomorphic maps \(f: \mathbb{CP}^1 \to X\) whose image represents a class \(\beta \in H_2(X, \mathbb{Z})\). The genus-zero Gromov–Witten invariant \(N_\beta\) (roughly) counts the number of such maps, weighted by signs from the obstruction theory.
For the quintic with \(h^{1,1} = 1\), the class \(\beta\) is determined by the degree \(d = \int_\beta \omega\), and the A-model genus-zero free energy takes the form \[
\mathcal{F}_A(t) = \frac{5}{6}t^3 + \sum_{d=1}^{\infty} N_d \, q^d, \qquad q = e^{2\pi i t},
\] where \(t\) is the complexified Kahler parameter and \(N_d\) is the genus-zero Gromov–Witten invariant at degree \(d\). The cubic term \(\frac{5}{6}t^3\) is the classical triple intersection number \(\int_X \omega^3 = 5\) (divided by \(3! = 6\)). The instanton sum \(\sum N_d q^d\) encodes the quantum corrections from holomorphic curves.
The relation between the Gromov–Witten invariants \(N_d\) and the “BPS numbers” \(n_d\) (the rational curve counts appearing in the prepotential formula with the trilogarithm) is given by the multi-cover formula: \[
N_d = \sum_{k | d} n_{d/k} \frac{1}{k^3}.
\] The integers \(n_d\) are the genuinely enumerative quantities, counting (in an appropriate sense) the number of isolated rational curves of degree \(d\).


The B-model: periods and variation of Hodge structure
The B-model on a Calabi–Yau \(\widetilde{X}\) depends only on the complex structure of \(\widetilde{X}\), and its observables are governed by the variation of Hodge structure (VHS) on the family of Calabi–Yau manifolds as the complex structure moduli vary. The central object is the holomorphic 3-form \(\Omega\) and its periods \(\Pi_i = \int_{\gamma_i} \Omega\).
As the complex structure moduli vary, \(\Omega\) traces out a path in the Hodge filtration \(F^3 \subset F^2 \subset F^1 \subset H^3(\widetilde{X}, \mathbb{C})\), and the B-model free energy is determined by the special geometry relations among the periods. The crucial point is that B-model computations are exact at tree level — there are no worldsheet instanton corrections on the B-model side. This is because the B-model path integral localizes on constant maps, and the moduli space of constant maps is just \(\widetilde{X}\) itself.


The mirror map and computational power
Mirror symmetry equates the A-model on \(X\) with the B-model on \(\widetilde{X}\): \[
\mathcal{F}_A^{X}(t) = \mathcal{F}_B^{\widetilde{X}}(\psi(t)).
\] The left side involves an infinite sum over worldsheet instantons (holomorphic curves), each of which is extremely difficult to compute directly on \(X\). The right side is a classical period computation on \(\widetilde{X}\), involving only ordinary differential equations (the Picard–Fuchs system). The mirror map \(t(\psi)\) relates the natural coordinates on the two sides.
This is the computational miracle: an infinite series of enumerative invariants, each requiring sophisticated algebraic geometry or symplectic topology to compute individually, is encoded in the solution of an ODE. For the quintic, this yields \(n_1 = 2875\) (the classical result of Schubert calculus), \(n_2 = 609{,}250\), \(n_3 = 317{,}206{,}375\), \(n_4 = 242{,}467{,}530{,}000\), and so on to arbitrarily high degree.

title: Mirror Symmetry and T-Duality
text:
D-Branes and Mirror Symmetry

Branes wrapping cycles
D-branes are extended objects on which open strings can end. A D\(p\)-brane in type II string theory wraps a \((p+1)\)-dimensional worldvolume. In a Calabi–Yau compactification:

Type IIA has D0, D2, D4, D6-branes wrapping even-dimensional cycles of \(X\).
Type IIB has D(-1), D1, D3, D5, D7-branes wrapping odd-dimensional cycles of \(X\).

Mirror symmetry exchanges the even and odd cycles. More precisely, it exchanges the A-branes (Lagrangian submanifolds, natural for type IIA) with B-branes (holomorphic submanifolds, natural for type IIB). In the SYZ picture, a D0-brane (a point) on \(X\) dualizes to a D3-brane wrapping the full \(T^3\) fiber on \(\widetilde{X}\), which is a special Lagrangian 3-cycle.


Calibrated geometry
The conditions for a D-brane to preserve supersymmetry are captured by calibrated geometry. A \(p\)-form \(\phi\) on a Riemannian manifold is a calibration if \(d\phi = 0\) and \(\phi|_{\Sigma} \leq \mathrm{vol}_\Sigma\) for every oriented \(p\)-dimensional submanifold \(\Sigma\). A submanifold saturating the bound is calibrated and minimizes volume in its homology class.
On a Calabi–Yau threefold, the relevant calibrations are:

\(\omega\) (the Kahler form) for holomorphic curves,
\(\frac{1}{2}\omega^2\) for holomorphic surfaces,
\(\mathrm{Re}(\Omega)\) for special Lagrangian 3-cycles.

Mirror symmetry exchanges the Kahler calibration data with the complex structure calibration data.

title: Mirror Symmetry and T-Duality
text:
Connections to Brane Tilings
For toric Calabi–Yau geometries — non-compact Calabi–Yau threefolds described by toric diagrams — mirror symmetry has a particularly explicit realization. The mirror of a toric Calabi–Yau singularity \(X\) can be written as a hypersurface \[
uv = W(x, y)
\] in \(\mathbb{C}^2 \times (\mathbb{C}^*)^2\), where the curve \(W(x,y) = 0\) is the mirror curve (or spectral curve). The toric data of \(X\) is encoded in the Newton polygon of \(W\).

From toric data to mirror curves
A toric Calabi–Yau threefold singularity is specified by a convex lattice polygon \(\Delta \subset \mathbb{Z}^2\) (the toric diagram). The mirror curve is a Riemann surface \(\Sigma\) embedded in \((\mathbb{C}^*)^2\), defined by a Laurent polynomial \[
W(x,y) = \sum_{(m,n) \in \Delta \cap \mathbb{Z}^2} a_{m,n} \, x^m y^n = 0,
\] whose Newton polygon is precisely \(\Delta\). The coefficients \(a_{m,n}\) encode the complex structure moduli of the mirror, which by mirror symmetry correspond to the Kahler moduli (resolution parameters and \(B\)-field periods) of \(X\). The genus of the mirror curve \(\Sigma\) equals the number of interior lattice points of \(\Delta\), which counts the number of compact 4-cycles in \(X\).


Brane tilings and the Kasteleyn matrix
Brane tilings (also called dimer models) provide a combinatorial bridge: a periodic bipartite graph \(\mathcal{G}\) on \(T^2\) encodes both the quiver gauge theory on D3-branes probing the toric singularity \(X\), and the geometry of the mirror. The faces of \(\mathcal{G}\) correspond to gauge group factors (nodes of the quiver), edges to bifundamental fields, and the bipartite structure determines the superpotential.
The connection to the mirror curve proceeds through the Kasteleyn matrix \(K(x,y)\). This is the weighted adjacency matrix of the bipartite graph, where each edge \(e\) connecting a black vertex \(b\) to a white vertex \(w\) receives a weight that includes reference fugacities \(x^{n_1(e)} y^{n_2(e)}\) tracking the homology class of the edge on \(T^2\). The characteristic polynomial of the Kasteleyn matrix, \[
P(x, y) = \det K(x, y),
\] is a Laurent polynomial in \(x\) and \(y\) whose zero locus \(P(x,y) = 0\) defines the mirror curve \(\Sigma\). The Newton polygon of \(P\) recovers the toric diagram \(\Delta\) of \(X\).
This gives a concrete and computational pipeline: starting from a brane tiling (which can be constructed systematically for any toric singularity), one reads off the Kasteleyn matrix, computes its determinant, and obtains the mirror curve together with its embedding in \((\mathbb{C}^*)^2\). The zig-zag paths of the tiling — oriented paths that turn maximally left at white vertices and maximally right at black vertices — are in bijection with the external legs of the toric diagram, providing a direct combinatorial map between the tiling and the toric geometry.


Example: the conifold
For the simplest non-trivial example, the conifold \(\mathcal{O}(-1) \oplus \mathcal{O}(-1) \to \mathbb{CP}^1\), the toric diagram is a line segment with two interior points, and the brane tiling is a square lattice on \(T^2\) with two faces. The Kasteleyn matrix is \(2 \times 2\): \[
K(x,y) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 + x \\ 1 + y \end{pmatrix}^T,
\] giving the mirror curve \(P(x,y) = 1 + x + y + xy = (1+x)(1+y)\). After a deformation by a complex structure parameter \(z\), this becomes \(P(x,y) = 1 + x + y + z\,xy\), a genus-0 curve whose periods encode the resolved conifold geometry.

title: Mirror Symmetry and T-Duality
text:
Homological Mirror Symmetry
In 1994, Kontsevich proposed a far-reaching mathematical formulation of mirror symmetry:
Kontsevich’s Homological Mirror Symmetry (HMS) Conjecture. For a mirror pair \((X, \widetilde{X})\) of Calabi–Yau manifolds, \[
D^b\mathrm{Coh}(X) \simeq D^\pi\mathrm{Fuk}(\widetilde{X}),
\] where \(D^b\mathrm{Coh}(X)\) is the bounded derived category of coherent sheaves on \(X\) (encoding B-branes), and \(D^\pi\mathrm{Fuk}(\widetilde{X})\) is the derived Fukaya category of \(\widetilde{X}\) (encoding A-branes, i.e., Lagrangian submanifolds with flat \(U(1)\) connections).
HMS elevates mirror symmetry from a statement about numbers (Hodge numbers, curve counts) to an equivalence of categorical structures. It has been proven in a number of cases, including elliptic curves (Polishchuk and Zaslow), the quartic K3 surface (Seidel), and toric varieties (various authors). The general case for compact Calabi–Yau threefolds remains open.
From the physics perspective, HMS is the statement that the open string sectors (D-brane categories) of the two mirror theories are equivalent, which is a natural consequence of the underlying string duality.

title: Mirror Symmetry and T-Duality
